anticoagulation.name: Anticoagulation management: INR and APTT
anticoagulation.overview: Every ward has patients on anticoagulants, and the exam tests whether you can interpret the monitoring tests (INR/APTT), match the drug to the indication, and reverse bleeding safely. The trap is choosing the wrong anticoagulant for a given scenario (e.g. a DOAC in a mechanical valve).
essentials: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X) plus proteins C and S. Full effect is delayed, so acute thrombosis needs bridging with a rapidly-acting agent (LMWH/heparin) until the INR is therapeutic.
Heparin (unfractionated) works via antithrombin III and is monitored by APTT; LMWH (enoxaparin) is weight-dosed and usually needs no monitoring. APTT is also prolonged in DIC and factor deficiencies.
Target INR: 2.0-3.0 for most indications (AF, VTE); 2.5-3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve or recurrent thrombosis on warfarin.
The route of monitoring drives the choice: warfarin needs regular INR; DOACs do not need routine monitoring but are contraindicated in mechanical valves and antiphospholipid syndrome.
Reversal is drug-specific: warfarin → vitamin K + PCC; heparin → protamine; dabigatran → idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors → andexanet alfa (or PCC if unavailable).

drugs.name: Warfarin
drugs.when: AF, VTE, mechanical heart valves, antiphospholipid syndrome
drugs.notes: Target INR 2-3 (2.5-3.5 mechanical mitral); needs monitoring; many food/drug interactions; teratogenic (avoid in pregnancy)

drugs.name: Apixaban / Rivaroxaban (Xa inhibitors)
drugs.when: Non-valvular AF; VTE treatment and prophylaxis; rivaroxaban also post-ACS
drugs.notes: No routine INR; dose-adjusted for renal function/age; contraindicated in mechanical valves and APS

drugs.name: Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor)
drugs.notes: Caution if CrCl <30; dyspepsia common; reversal = idarucizumab

drugs.name: Edoxaban
drugs.when: Non-valvular AF; VTE (after initial parenteral therapy)
drugs.notes: Reduce dose if CrCl 15-50

drugs.name: LMWH (enoxaparin)
drugs.when: VTE treatment/prophylaxis; pregnancy (drug of choice); cancer-associated VTE; bridging warfarin
drugs.notes: Weight-based; reduce/avoid if CrCl <30; monitor anti-Xa only in special cases (pregnancy, renal impairment, obesity)

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
drugs.when: ACS; when rapid on/off is needed; severe renal impairment; during procedures
drugs.notes: Monitor APTT (target 1.5-2.5x control); reversal = protamine sulfate

drugs.name: Reversal agents
drugs.notes: Warfarin → IV vitamin K + PCC; heparin → protamine; dabigatran → idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors → andexanet alfa

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A 70-year-old with AF has a mechanical mitral valve. Which anticoagulant?
clinicalScenarios.answer: Warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5). DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A pregnant woman (12 weeks) has a confirmed DVT.
clinicalScenarios.answer: LMWH — it does not cross the placenta. Warfarin (teratogenic) and DOACs (avoid) are contraindicated.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: New AF in a 62-year-old with normal renal function and no valve disease.
clinicalScenarios.answer: A DOAC is now preferred over warfarin (no monitoring, fewer interactions); anticoagulate per CHA2DS2-VASc.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: INR 8.4 with no bleeding.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Withhold warfarin, give oral vitamin K, recheck INR. No PCC unless bleeding.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: INR 6.8 with haematemesis and hypotension.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Major bleeding — IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) + resuscitate.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: AF with CrCl 20 mL/min.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Apixaban (dose-reduced) or warfarin; avoid dabigatran (renally cleared).

keyValues: INR therapeutic (mechanical mitral valve, recurrent VTE)
redFlags: Major bleeding on any anticoagulant (intracranial, GI, retroperitoneal) — reverse urgently, don't just withhold.
INR > 5.0 with bleeding — emergency, give PCC.
New thrombosis despite therapeutic anticoagulation — consider compliance, drug interaction, or occult malignancy.
management: Bleeding on warfarin: stop warfarin, IV vitamin K, PCC, recheck INR.
Bleeding on heparin: stop infusion, give protamine sulfate.
Bleeding on dabigatran: idarucizumab. On a Xa inhibitor: andexanet alfa.
Subtherapeutic INR with high thrombotic risk: re-dose warfarin, consider bridging with LMWH.
Always check for interacting drugs (antibiotics, amiodarone, NSAIDs) when INR swings.
pitfalls: DOACs are NOT interchangeable with warfarin — they are contraindicated in mechanical valves and antiphospholipid syndrome.
Warfarin takes days for full effect — never rely on it alone for acute thrombosis.
APTT does not monitor DOACs or warfarin — don't be misled by a normal APTT in a patient on apixaban.

chest-pain.name: Chest pain
chest-pain.overview: Chest pain is a 'rule out the killers first' topic. The exam expects you to identify ACS and the other immediately life-threatening causes within the first minutes, then treat.
essentials: First exclude the life-threatening causes: acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, oesophageal rupture.
ACS: central crushing pain radiating to arm/jaw, with sweating/nausea; may be atypical in women, diabetics and the elderly. ECG changes + troponin rise confirm.
Aortic dissection: sudden severe 'tearing' pain radiating to the back, with a pulse/BP differential and widened mediastinum — a surgical emergency.
PE: pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, hypoxia, tachycardia, with risk factors (immobility, surgery, malignancy, OCP).
Non-cardiac causes: musculoskeletal, GORD, anxiety, and pericarditis (positional/pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward).

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.notes: 300 mg chewed/loading dose — give early unless true allergy

drugs.name: GTN / nitrates
drugs.notes: Contraindicated in hypotension, severe aortic stenosis, and on PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil)

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.when: Severe ischaemic pain unresponsive to nitrates
drugs.notes: IV, titrated; may cause hypotension and vomiting

drugs.name: Beta-blocker
drugs.when: ACS (if no contraindication), aortic dissection (rate control)
drugs.notes: Avoid in cardiogenic shock, severe asthma, high-grade heart block

drugs.name: Anticoagulant (LMWH/heparin)
drugs.notes: Per ACS pathway; do not delay reperfusion for it

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 58-year-old, central crushing chest pain, ST elevation in II/III/aVF.
clinicalScenarios.answer: STEMI — activate primary PCI immediately; give aspirin. Do not wait for troponin.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 65-year-old, sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, 30 mmHg BP difference between arms.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Aortic dissection — control BP/HR with a beta-blocker, urgent CT aortogram, surgical referral.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 30-year-old on the OCP with pleuritic pain, dyspnoea and hypoxia.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Suspected PE — Wells score, CTPA (or D-dimer if low probability), anticoagulate if high probability.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Sharp pleuritic pain worse lying flat, relieved by leaning forward, with a rub.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Pericarditis — NSAIDs + colchicine; look for a cause (viral, post-MI, autoimmune).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Chest pain that is worse on palpation and movement, in a well 25-year-old.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Musculoskeletal — reassure and treat symptomatically after excluding serious causes.

keyValues: Rises 3-6 h after ACS; use serial samples/high-sensitivity assay
Primary PCI within 120 min of diagnosis
Negative rules out PE in low/intermediate probability
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability + new murmur / unequal pulses — think dissection.
ST elevation — STEMI pathway (primary PCI).
Chest pain with hypoxia and tachycardia — consider PE.
management: Immediate: ABC, oxygen only if hypoxic, IV access, 12-lead ECG within 10 min, cardiac monitoring.
ACS: aspirin, nitrates, analgesia; antiplatelet + anticoagulant per pathway; STEMI → primary PCI.
Dissection: heart-rate/BP control (beta-blocker), urgent CT aortogram, cardiothoracic surgery.
PE: risk-stratify (Wells), D-dimer/CTPA, LMWH if high probability.
Pericarditis: NSAIDs + colchicine.
pitfalls: A normal troponin early does not exclude ACS — repeat it.
Do not give nitrates in hypotension or suspected severe aortic stenosis.
'Tearing' to the back + BP differential = dissection, not ACS — the treatments differ.

arrhythmias.name: Common arrhythmias
arrhythmias.overview: The first branch point in any arrhythmia is haemodynamic stability: unstable = electricity (cardioversion/pacing), stable = drugs and rate/rhythm control. The exam tests AF, SVT, VT and bradyarrhythmias.
essentials: Assess stability first: an unstable patient with any tachy- or bradyarrhythmia needs urgent treatment (synchronised DC cardioversion or pacing), not just drugs.
Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular. Causes: ischaemia, sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol, valvular disease. Manage rate (beta-blocker/CCB) or rhythm, and assess stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc).
SVT (AVNRT/AVRT): regular narrow-complex tachycardia — vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine, then CCB/beta-blocker.
VT: broad-complex tachycardia — pulseless → arrest algorithm; stable → amiodarone/lidocaine and treat the cause (ischaemia, electrolytes).
Bradyarrhythmias and heart block: if symptomatic/unstable → atropine then pacing; complete heart block needs pacing.

drugs.name: Adenosine
drugs.notes: 6 mg then 12 mg rapid IV bolus; warn about transient chest tightness/flushing; avoid in severe asthma

drugs.name: Bisoprolol / metoprolol (beta-blocker)
drugs.notes: Avoid in severe asthma, decompensated heart failure, high-grade block

drugs.name: Diltiazem / verapamil (CCB)
drugs.when: AF rate control, SVT (if no heart failure)
drugs.notes: Avoid in heart failure with reduced EF and in broad-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.when: Stable VT, AF rhythm control; during cardiac arrest (shockable)
drugs.notes: 300 mg IV over 10-20 min in arrest; long-term: thyroid/lung/liver toxicity

drugs.name: Digoxin
drugs.when: Rate control in AF, especially with heart failure or sedentary patients
drugs.notes: Narrow therapeutic window; renal clearance

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.notes: 500 mcg IV, repeat to 3 mg; then pacing

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.notes: IV; correct K+ and Mg2+

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Irregularly irregular pulse, rate 110, haemodynamically stable.
clinicalScenarios.answer: AF — rate control (beta-blocker/CCB) + assess CHA2DS2-VASc for anticoagulation.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180, hypotensive and dizzy.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Unstable SVT — synchronised DC cardioversion (not adenosine).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180, stable.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Vagal manoeuvres → adenosine 6 mg → 12 mg → CCB/beta-blocker.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Broad-complex tachycardia, no pulse.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Pulseless VT — defibrillate immediately, CPR, adrenaline per ALS.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Complete heart block with syncope.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Atropine then transcutaneous/transvenous pacing; involve cardiology.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Polymorphic VT in a patient on QT-prolonging drugs.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Torsades de pointes — IV magnesium, stop the culprit drug, correct K+/Mg2+.

redFlags: Pulseless VT/VF — defibrillate immediately.
Unstable tachyarrhythmia (shock, chest pain, syncope, heart failure) — synchronised cardioversion.
Complete heart block with bradycardia — pacing.
management: Unstable: synchronised DC cardioversion (tachy) or atropine/pacing (brady).
Stable AF: rate control (beta-blocker/CCB); anticoagulate per score; consider rhythm control if symptomatic/recent onset.
Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres → adenosine → CCB/beta-blocker.
Stable VT: amiodarone/lidocaine, correct electrolytes, treat ischaemia.
Torsades: IV magnesium, stop QT-prolonging drugs.
pitfalls: Don't cardiovert a stable patient or drug-treat an unstable one — stability decides the route.
Verapamil/diltiazem are dangerous in broad-complex tachycardia you think might be VT.
Always anticoagulate AF per stroke risk, not just control the rate.

collapse-shock.name: Collapse and shock
collapse-shock.overview: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion — not just a low BP. The exam expects you to classify the type (hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive) because the treatment differs completely.
essentials: Shock = inadequate tissue perfusion. Types: hypovolaemic (haemorrhage, dehydration), cardiogenic (MI, arrhythmia, tamponade), obstructive (PE, tension pneumothorax), distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis).
Recognise early: tachycardia, cool peripheries, prolonged capillary refill, reduced urine output, altered consciousness, rising lactate — BP falls late.
Hypovolaemic shock is the most common — treat with rapid fluid/blood and control the source of loss.
Cardiogenic shock is pump failure — adding fluid can worsen it; needs inotropes and treatment of the cause.
Septic shock is distributive — early antibiotics + fluids + lactate-guided resuscitation (Sepsis Six).

drugs.name: IV crystalloid (balanced)
drugs.notes: 250-500 mL boluses, reassess after each; avoid in cardiogenic shock

drugs.name: Blood products
drugs.notes: Cross-matched or O-negative in extremis; activate major haemorrhage protocol

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (vasopressor)
drugs.when: Septic shock not responding to fluids; MAP target ≥65
drugs.notes: Central line preferred; first-line vasopressor

drugs.name: Adrenaline
drugs.notes: Anaphylaxis: 500 mcg IM anterolateral thigh

drugs.name: Dobutamine (inotrope)
drugs.notes: Increases contractility; monitor for arrhythmia

drugs.name: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
drugs.notes: Within 1 hour; per local policy

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Stab wound to the abdomen, hypotensive, tachycardic, cool peripheries.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Haemorrhagic (hypovolaemic) shock — rapid fluids/blood + urgent surgery; don't delay for imaging.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-MI patient with hypotension, crackles, raised JVP.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Cardiogenic shock — cautious fluids, inotropes, treat ischaemia/arrhythmia; fluids alone worsen it.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Sepsis with lactate 4.2 and hypotension.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Septic shock — Sepsis Six within 1 hour; noradrenaline if MAP <65 despite fluids.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Sudden collapse with absent breath sounds on one side and tracheal shift.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Tension pneumothorax — immediate needle decompression, then chest drain.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Collapse after a bee sting with wheeze and hypotension.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline 500 mcg, high-flow oxygen, IV fluids.

redFlags: Unresponsive or agonal breathing — cardiac arrest pathway.
Tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, tracheal shift) — needle decompression.
Cardiac tamponade (muffled heart sounds, raised JVP, hypotension) — pericardiocentesis.
management: ABC, high-flow oxygen, IV access, monitoring, treat the specific cause.
Hypovolaemic: rapid crystalloid/blood, control haemorrhage.
Septic: Sepsis Six — cultures, antibiotics, fluids, lactate; noradrenaline if refractory.
Cardiogenic: treat arrhythmia/ischaemia, cautious fluids, inotropes, cardiology review.
pitfalls: BP is a late sign — a normal BP does not exclude shock; use lactate, urine output and perfusion.
Giving large fluid boluses in cardiogenic shock can precipitate pulmonary oedema.
Do not wait for imaging before treating tension pneumothorax or haemorrhage.

syncope.name: Syncope
syncope.overview: Syncope = transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid spontaneous recovery. The exam's key skill is separating benign reflex syncope from dangerous cardiac syncope.
essentials: Syncope is transient LOC due to cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid recovery. Distinguish from seizure (post-ictal confusion, tongue biting, tonic-clonic movements) and drop attacks (no LOC).
Reflex (vasovagal) syncope is most common — triggered by pain, emotion, standing or micturition, with a prodrome of light-headedness, sweating, nausea.
Orthostatic hypotension: on standing, especially in the elderly, dehydrated, or on antihypertensives.
Cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, HCM, PE) is the dangerous type — may occur on exertion with no prodrome.
Investigations: ECG, lying/standing BP, echo, Holter, tilt test. Admit if a cardiac cause is suspected.

drugs.name: Midodrine / fludrocortisone
drugs.notes: Vasoconstrictor/volume expander; specialist initiation

drugs.name: IV fluids
drugs.notes: Crystalloid; treat the underlying cause

drugs.name: Rate/rhythm drugs
drugs.notes: Per cardiology; pacemaker for bradyarrhythmic syncope

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Young woman faints after a blood test, with light-headedness and sweating, quick recovery.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Vasovagal (reflex) syncope — reassure, fluids, avoid triggers, counter-pressure manoeuvres.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 55-year-old collapses on exertion with no prodrome; father died suddenly at 50.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Suspected cardiac syncope — ECG + cardiology assessment (arrhythmia, HCM, aortic stenosis).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Elderly patient faints on standing shortly after starting an antihypertensive.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Orthostatic hypotension — review drugs, lying/standing BP, hydration.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Witnessed collapse with tongue biting and post-ictal confusion.
clinicalScenarios.answer: This is a seizure, not syncope — investigate for epilepsy/cause (EEG, imaging, glucose).

keyValues: Heart block, long QT, Brugada pattern, ischaemia
Exertional, no prodrome, family history of sudden death, abnormal ECG
Group 1: stop driving after unexplained syncope until assessed
redFlags: Syncope during exertion — think cardiac.
Abnormal ECG, structural heart disease, or family history of sudden cardiac death.
Recurrent unexplained syncope — needs cardiology assessment.
management: ABC, check glucose, ECG, lying/standing BP.
Reassure and advise for reflex syncope (fluids, avoid triggers, counter-pressure manoeuvres).
Cardiac syncope: treat the arrhythmia/structural cause; admit for monitoring.
Advise driving restrictions per DVLA after syncope.
pitfalls: Exertional syncope with no prodrome = cardiac until proven otherwise.
A 'funny turn' with a long post-ictal phase is more likely a seizure.
Always check lying/standing BP — orthostatic hypotension is easy to miss.

acute-limb-ischaemia.name: Acute limb ischaemia
acute-limb-ischaemia.overview: A time-critical vascular emergency — irreversible damage begins within hours. The exam tests recognising the '6 Ps' and knowing not to delay the vascular team for imaging.
essentials: Acute limb ischaemia = sudden loss of limb perfusion, usually embolism (AF, recent MI) or in-situ thrombosis (atherosclerosis). The '6 Ps': pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishing cold.
Time-critical: irreversible muscle/nerve damage within 4-6 hours. Paralysis and paraesthesia indicate advanced ischaemia.
Embolic (sudden, no prior claudication, normal contralateral pulses) vs thrombotic (background of chronic peripheral arterial disease).
Examine and document: pulses (femoral, popliteal, DP, PT), capillary refill, sensation, motor function, level of the block.
Immediate: heparin, analgesia, keep the limb warm, urgent vascular referral — do not delay for imaging if the limb is threatened.

drugs.name: IV unfractionated heparin
drugs.when: Immediate, once acute limb ischaemia is suspected
drugs.notes: Prevents clot propagation; give before imaging/surgery

drugs.name: Analgesia (opioid)
drugs.notes: IV titrated morphine

drugs.name: Thrombolysis (intra-arterial alteplase)
drugs.notes: Catheter-directed; watch for bleeding/reperfusion injury

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 78-year-old with AF: sudden painful, pale, cold right leg with absent pulses and no prior claudication.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Acute embolic limb ischaemia — IV heparin, analgesia, urgent vascular surgery.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Acutely ischaemic leg with new paralysis and paraesthesia.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Advanced ischaemia with imminent irreversible damage — immediate vascular review; do not delay for imaging.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A patient known to have claudication develops sudden worsening rest pain and mottling.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Acute-on-chronic (thrombotic) ischaemia — anticoagulate and refer urgently.

keyValues: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishing cold
IV heparin, analgesia, urgent vascular review
Watch for compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis
redFlags: Paralysis or paraesthesia — advanced ischaemia, imminent irreversible damage.
Cold, mottled, pulseless limb — surgical emergency.
Rhabdomyolysis after reperfusion — check K+ and CK, watch renal function.
management: ABC, IV heparin, analgesia, keep the limb warm, NBM, urgent vascular referral.
Do not delay for imaging if the limb is threatened.
Post-reperfusion: monitor for compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis.
pitfalls: Do not elevate the limb or apply heat — keep it warm and dependent but not raised.
A 'pulseless leg' is not the same as chronic claudication — the sudden onset is the clue.
Never wait for an angiogram in a threatened limb — the vascular team decides.

chronic-limb-ischaemia.name: Chronic limb ischaemia – ulcers and gangrene
chronic-limb-ischaemia.overview: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and the diabetic foot are common ward problems. The exam tests recognising the type of ulcer and knowing when to escalate (infection, gangrene).
essentials: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI): rest pain, non-healing ulcers, or gangrene due to peripheral arterial disease. Rest pain is worse at night, relieved by hanging the leg down.
Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, age. Diabetic foot disease involves both neuropathic and ischaemic components.
Ulcer types: arterial (punched-out, painful, pale base, on toes/heel), venous (gaiter area, shallow, wet, painless), neuropathic (plantar, painless, at pressure points).
Assess: ABPI, pulses, monofilament sensation, ulcer characteristics, signs of infection.
Management: best medical therapy, revascularisation for CLTI, wound care, and amputation if unsalvageable.

drugs.name: Antiplatelet (clopidogrel/aspirin)
drugs.notes: Secondary prevention; part of best medical therapy

drugs.name: Statin (atorvastatin)
drugs.notes: High-intensity dose regardless of cholesterol level

drugs.name: Antibiotics
drugs.notes: Per local policy; wound swab; IV if systemically unwell

drugs.name: Analgesia
drugs.notes: Regular paracetamol/opioid; improve perfusion to relieve it

drugs.name: Prostanoids / specialist agents
drugs.notes: Iloprost in selected patients

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Diabetic with a painless punched-out plantar ulcer and loss of monofilament sensation.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Neuropathic (diabetic) ulcer — offloading, podiatry, glycaemic control.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Rest pain and ABPI 0.4 with a non-healing heel ulcer.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia — best medical therapy + vascular referral for revascularisation.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Diabetic foot ulcer with crepitus, spreading infection and fever.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Necrotising infection — IV antibiotics + urgent surgical debridement.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Deep ulcer with positive probe-to-bone.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Suspect osteomyelitis — MRI, prolonged antibiotics, consider amputation.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Painless shallow ulcer in the gaiter area with surrounding pigmentation and oedema.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Venous ulcer — compression therapy, wound care, elevate the leg.

keyValues: >0.9 normal; <0.5 severe ischaemia; >1.3 suggests calcified vessels (diabetes)
Worse at night, relieved by dependency
redFlags: Gangrene or necrotic tissue — urgent vascular review, possible amputation.
Infected diabetic foot with systemic sepsis — emergency, IV antibiotics + debridement.
Rapid deterioration or acute-on-chronic ischaemia.
management: Best medical therapy: antiplatelet, statin, smoking cessation, tight diabetes/BP control.
CLTI: refer to vascular surgery for revascularisation.
Infected ulcer: swab, antibiotics, debridement, offloading (diabetic).
Wound care: keep clean, moist, offload pressure; tissue viability/podiatry.
pitfalls: A painless ulcer is not always benign — in diabetes it is neuropathic and risk of infection is high.
An ABPI >1.3 in diabetes is falsely reassuring — vessels are calcified; use toe pressures.
Do not use compression on an ischaemic (arterial) ulcer.

dvt-pe.name: Deep Venous thrombosis and Pulmonary embolism
dvt-pe.overview: VTE is a spectrum (DVT → PE) and a top cause of preventable hospital death. The exam tests risk stratification (Wells), the D-dimer vs imaging decision, and treating massive PE.
essentials: VTE = DVT + PE, one disease. Risk factors: immobility, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy/OCP, thrombophilia, previous VTE, obesity.
DVT: unilateral leg swelling, pain, erythema, warmth, dilated superficial veins. Wells score; D-dimer rules out in low probability; USS confirms.
PE: dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, hypoxia, tachycardia, haemoptysis, collapse. Massive PE → obstructive shock.
Anticoagulation is the mainstay (LMWH → DOAC or warfarin); massive PE with shock → thrombolysis.
Prevention: VTE prophylaxis (LMWH, TEDs, early mobilisation) for all at-risk inpatients.

drugs.name: LMWH (enoxaparin)
drugs.when: Initial treatment of confirmed/high-probability VTE; VTE prophylaxis; pregnancy; cancer-associated VTE
drugs.notes: Weight-based; reduce in renal impairment

drugs.name: DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban)
drugs.notes: No monitoring; avoid in APS/mechanical valves

drugs.name: Warfarin
drugs.when: Long-term VTE (with initial LMWH bridging), APS
drugs.notes: Target INR 2-3; needs monitoring

drugs.name: Alteplase (thrombolysis)
drugs.notes: IV bolus/infusion; contraindicated in recent surgery/bleeding

drugs.name: VTE prophylaxis
drugs.notes: LMWH + mechanical (TEDs/compression); early mobilisation

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 30-year-old on the OCP with sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain and hypoxia; Wells 5.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Suspected PE with high Wells — CTPA (not D-dimer); anticoagulate if high probability while awaiting.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Confirmed massive PE with hypotension and shock.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Thrombolysis (alteplase); consider surgical/mechanical embolectomy.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Unilateral leg swelling after a long-haul flight; Wells 3.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Likely DVT — USS; anticoagulate if high probability while awaiting.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-operative patient with a low Wells score for PE.
clinicalScenarios.answer: D-dimer — a negative result rules out PE in low/intermediate probability.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Cancer patient with a recurrent VTE.
clinicalScenarios.answer: LMWH is preferred over DOACs in cancer-associated thrombosis (per guidance).

keyValues: Negative rules out VTE in low/intermediate probability
3 months (provoked); longer/indefinite if unprovoked or cancer
redFlags: PE with hypotension/shock — massive PE, thrombolyse.
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (tense, blue, painful leg) — venous gangrene risk.
Sudden collapse with risk factors — consider PE.
management: Suspected DVT: Wells score, D-dimer, USS; anticoagulate if high probability.
Suspected PE: Wells, D-dimer/CTPA, LMWH if high probability.
Confirmed VTE: therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH → DOAC or warfarin), duration by cause.
Massive PE: thrombolysis; consider embolectomy.
Prevention: LMWH + TEDs + early mobilisation for at-risk inpatients.
pitfalls: Do not order D-dimer when Wells is high — go straight to imaging.
Massive PE with shock needs thrombolysis, not just heparin.
In pregnancy, imaging (CTPA or V/Q) — do not avoid it out of radiation concern.

shortness-of-breath.name: Shortness of breath
shortness-of-breath.overview: Dyspnoea is the most common acute medical presentation — the exam wants you to pick out the immediately life-threatening causes (PE, tension pneumothorax, severe asthma, pulmonary oedema, anaphylaxis) and treat before you diagnose.
essentials: Life-threatening causes to exclude first: PE, tension pneumothorax, severe asthma/COPD, acute pulmonary oedema, anaphylaxis, foreign body.
Assess severity: ability to speak in sentences, accessory muscle use, respiratory rate, saturations, ABG. A silent chest in asthma is ominous (no air entry).
Pulmonary oedema (heart failure): orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, basal crackles, raised JVP, S3 — treat with oxygen, diuretics, nitrates, CPAP.
COPD exacerbation: increased breathlessness, wheeze, sputum change — bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics if infective, controlled oxygen.
Pneumothorax: sudden pleuritic pain + dyspnoea; tension variant (tracheal shift, haemodynamic compromise) needs immediate needle decompression.

drugs.name: Salbutamol (nebulised)
drugs.notes: 2.5-5 mg; titrate; watch for tremor and hypokalaemia

drugs.name: Ipratropium (nebulised)
drugs.notes: Add to salbutamol; 500 mcg

drugs.name: Prednisolone / hydrocortisone
drugs.notes: Oral prednisolone 40-50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone)

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.notes: IV 1.2-2 g over 20 min

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.notes: IV 40-80 mg; monitor urine output and renal function

drugs.name: Nitrates (GTN)
drugs.notes: IV/oral; avoid if hypotensive

drugs.name: Antibiotics
drugs.notes: Per local policy if increased sputum purulence

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnoea with unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation in an unstable patient.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Tension pneumothorax — immediate needle decompression (2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular), then chest drain.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Orthopnoea with bibasal crackles, raised JVP and a third heart sound.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Acute pulmonary oedema — oxygen, IV furosemide, nitrates, consider CPAP.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Asthma patient with a silent chest and drowsiness.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Near-fatal asthma — call for help, nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, steroids, IV magnesium; consider ICU.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: COPD patient with purulent sputum, increased breathlessness and wheeze.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Infective exacerbation — controlled oxygen (88-92%), bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Elderly patient with sudden dyspnoea, hypoxia and tachycardia after recent surgery.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider PE — Wells score, CTPA, anticoagulate if high probability.

keyValues: Cannot complete sentences, RR>25, HR>110, PEF<50%
redFlags: Silent chest, exhaustion, or reduced consciousness in asthma — peri-arrest.
Tension pneumothorax — decompress immediately, do not wait for X-ray.
Hypoxia refractory to oxygen — think PE, shunt, or severe disease.
management: ABC, target oxygen, sit the patient up, IV access, monitoring.
Asthma: salbutamol, ipratropium, steroids, magnesium; escalate if severe.
Pulmonary oedema: furosemide, nitrates, CPAP, treat the cause.
Pneumothorax: aspirate or drain per size/clinical state; tension → decompress first.
pitfalls: Do not give uncontrolled high-flow oxygen to a COPD patient at risk of hypercapnia.
A normal chest X-ray does not exclude PE — go on to CTPA if clinical suspicion is high.
In tension pneumothorax, treat clinically — imaging would delay life-saving decompression.

oxygen-management.name: Oxygen management in wards
oxygen-management.overview: Oxygen is a drug: it needs a prescribed target, an appropriate device, and monitoring. The exam tests the two targets (94-98% vs 88-92%) and the danger of over-oxygenating COPD.
essentials: Prescribe oxygen with a target saturation range, not 'as required'. Over-oxygenation in COPD can suppress the hypoxic drive and cause hypercapnia.
Targets: 94-98% for most acutely ill patients; 88-92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease).
Delivery devices: nasal cannulae (low flow), simple face mask, Venturi mask (precise FiO2, 24-60%), non-rebreathe mask (high flow ~15 L/min) for emergencies.
Monitor the response: saturations and ABG if hypercapnia is suspected or the target is not met. Reassess regularly.
Document the prescription, target range, device, and a weaning plan; escalate if saturations fall below target.

drugs.name: Oxygen (nasal cannulae)
drugs.notes: 1-6 L/min; ~24-44% FiO2 (variable)

drugs.name: Venturi mask
drugs.notes: 24%, 28%, 35%, 40%, 60% — controlled delivery

drugs.name: Non-rebreathe mask
drugs.notes: 15 L/min, ~85-95% FiO2; humidify if prolonged

drugs.name: NIV (BiPAP/CPAP)
drugs.when: Hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD) or type 2 failure
drugs.notes: Consider if pH<7.35 and PaCO2 high; strict monitoring

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Known COPD with an exacerbation, saturations 90% on air.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Controlled oxygen to 88-92% via Venturi mask; recheck ABG (risk of CO2 retention).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A healthy 30-year-old with pneumonia and saturations 90%.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Target 94-98%; titrate oxygen and treat the pneumonia; check ABG if not improving.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: COPD patient on high-flow oxygen becomes drowsy with a rising PaCO2.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Reduce FiO2 to target 88-92%, check ABG, consider NIV — this is hypercapnic respiratory failure.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Saturations 85% despite a non-rebreathe mask at 15 L/min.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Refractory hypoxia — call for help, ABG, look for the cause (PE, pneumothorax, oedema, shunt).

redFlags: Falling saturations despite high-flow oxygen — call for help, consider ABG.
Rising CO2 or drowsiness in COPD on oxygen — reduce FiO2, consider NIV.
Hypoxia with no improvement — look for the cause rather than simply increasing flow.
management: Prescribe oxygen with a target range and device.
Start at an appropriate FiO2 and titrate to target; monitor saturations.
Check ABG if hypercapnia risk or the target is not achieved.
Wean oxygen as the patient improves; document the plan.
pitfalls: 'Oxygen as required' is not a prescription — always state a target range and device.
Beware over-oxygenation in COPD — high flow can cause dangerous CO2 retention.
Do not delay NIV in hypercapnic respiratory failure while waiting for a repeat ABG.

abg-interpretation.name: Arterial blood gas interpretation
abg-interpretation.overview: ABGs are examined constantly — the exam expects a systematic read (oxygenation → pH → PaCO2 → HCO3 → compensation) and matching the pattern to a cause.
essentials: Systematic approach: (1) oxygenation (PaO2), (2) pH (acidaemia/alkalaemia), (3) PaCO2 (respiratory), (4) HCO3 (metabolic), (5) compensation.
Respiratory acidosis: high PaCO2 (hypoventilation — COPD, sedation, neuromuscular). Respiratory alkalosis: low PaCO2 (hyperventilation — pain, anxiety, PE, sepsis).
Metabolic acidosis: low HCO3 — anion gap (lactate, ketoacidosis, renal failure, toxins) vs non-anion gap (diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis).
Metabolic alkalosis: high HCO3 (vomiting, diuretics, hypokalaemia).
Compensation: respiratory compensates metabolic quickly (change in PaCO2); metabolic compensates respiratory slowly (change in HCO3). Check whether compensation is adequate.

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.notes: Titrate to target; beware CO2 retention in COPD

drugs.name: Naloxone
drugs.notes: IV; reverses sedation/hypoventilation

drugs.name: NIV (BiPAP)
drugs.notes: Reduces PaCO2 and work of breathing; monitor closely

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.notes: Reserved for e.g. TCA toxicity or severe acidaemia; not routine

clinicalScenarios.scenario: pH 7.28, PaCO2 8.0 kPa, HCO3 24.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Respiratory acidosis (hypoventilation) — improve ventilation, treat the cause.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: pH 7.30, PaCO2 3.5 kPa, HCO3 12, lactate 6.
clinicalScenarios.answer: High anion-gap metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis) — look for sepsis/ischaemia, resuscitate.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: pH 7.48, PaCO2 3.0 kPa, HCO3 24 in an anxious patient with a PE.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation) — treat the underlying cause (PE, pain, sepsis).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: pH 7.50, HCO3 32 in a patient who has been vomiting.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Metabolic alkalosis — replace fluids/electrolytes, treat the cause.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: pH 7.20, PaCO2 6.5, HCO3 18 in a COPD patient.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Decompensated respiratory acidosis — consider NIV, controlled oxygen; this is type 2 respiratory failure.

redFlags: pH < 7.2 — severe acidaemia, consider ICU/bicarbonate.
Lactic acidosis (lactate >4) — sepsis/ischaemia, treat the cause.
Rising PaCO2 with falling pH in COPD — hypercapnic respiratory failure, consider NIV.
management: Interpret systematically: oxygenation → pH → PaCO2 → HCO3 → compensation.
Treat the underlying cause, not just the numbers.
Respiratory acidosis: improve ventilation (bronchodilators, NIV, treat cause).
Metabolic acidosis: identify the anion gap and treat the cause (fluids, insulin for DKA, sepsis).
pitfalls: Always check compensation — a normal pH can hide a mixed picture.
Calculate the anion gap in every metabolic acidosis — it points to the cause.
A normal PaO2 on oxygen can mask severe disease — interpret in context of FiO2.

electrolytes.name: Electrolyte management
electrolytes.overview: Electrolyte emergencies (especially hypo/hyperkalaemia) cause arrhythmias and arrest. The exam tests safe correction — rate of change matters as much as the target.
essentials: Sodium: hyponatraemia (common) — assess volume status and osmolality; causes include SIADH, hypovolaemia, heart failure, adrenal insufficiency. Correct slowly (risk of osmotic demyelination). Hypernatraemia = water deficit.
Potassium: hypokalaemia (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea) risks arrhythmia — replace. Hyperkalaemia (renal failure, ACEi, K+-sparing diuretics, cell lysis) is a cardiac emergency.
Calcium: hypercalcaemia (malignancy, hyperparathyroidism) — hydrate + bisphosphonate. Hypocalcaemia (post-thyroidectomy, hypoparathyroidism) — tetany, Chvostek/Trousseau signs.
Magnesium: hypomagnesaemia (diuretics, alcohol) associates with hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia and arrhythmia; hypermagnesaemia occurs in renal failure.
Phosphate: hypophosphataemia (refeeding, dialysis) causes muscle weakness and rhabdomyolysis.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate 10%
drugs.notes: IV 10-30 mL; stabilises myocardium but does not lower K+

drugs.name: Insulin + dextrose
drugs.notes: Shifts K+ into cells; monitor glucose closely

drugs.name: Salbutamol (nebulised)
drugs.notes: Shifts K+ intracellularly

drugs.name: Potassium chloride
drugs.notes: Oral or IV (max 10 mmol/h peripherally, 20 mmol/h central with monitoring)

drugs.name: Spironolactone / furosemide
drugs.notes: K+-sparing vs K+-wasting — choose to correct the K+

drugs.name: IV fluids / bisphosphonate
drugs.notes: Aggressive saline + zoledronic acid/pamidronate

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.notes: IV; often needed alongside K+ replacement

clinicalScenarios.scenario: K+ 7.0 with peaked T waves on ECG.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Hyperkalaemia emergency — calcium gluconate (myocardial protection), insulin+dextrose, salbutamol, then removal (resonium/dialysis).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: K+ 2.8 on a thiazide diuretic.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Hypokalaemia — replace K+ (oral/IV) and review the diuretic; check Mg2+.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Na+ 118 with confusion and seizures.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Severe hyponatraemia — hypertonic saline for seizures, but correct slowly (≤8-10 mmol/L/24 h) to avoid osmotic demyelination.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-thyroidectomy patient with tingling and muscle twitching.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Hypocalcaemia — IV calcium gluconate; check corrected calcium, magnesium and PTH.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Malignancy patient with confusion, thirst and a calcium of 3.2 mmol/L.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Hypercalcaemia — IV fluids then a bisphosphonate; treat the underlying malignancy.

redFlags: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T, wide QRS) — treat immediately.
Severe hyponatraemia with seizures — hypertonic saline, but correct slowly.
Symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, laryngospasm) — IV calcium.
management: Hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate (protection), insulin+dextrose, salbutamol, then K+ removal.
Hypokalaemia: oral/IV potassium replacement and treat the cause; check magnesium.
Hyponatraemia: treat the cause and correct slowly with frequent monitoring.
Hypercalcaemia: IV fluids, bisphosphonate, treat malignancy.
pitfalls: Calcium gluconate protects the heart but does not lower potassium — always follow with a shifting/removal strategy.
Correcting hyponatraemia too fast causes osmotic demyelination — go slowly.
Always check magnesium when treating hypokalaemia — low Mg2+ makes K+ hard to correct.

low-urine-output.name: Low urine output
low-urine-output.overview: Oliguria is a common ward call and often reversible. The exam tests classifying AKI (pre-renal / intrinsic / post-renal) and the safe first step.
essentials: Oliguria = urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h (or <400 mL/24h). Anuria (<100 mL/24h) suggests obstruction or severe renal failure.
Classify AKI: pre-renal (hypovolaemia, sepsis, heart failure — most common), intrinsic renal (ATN, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis), post-renal (obstruction — catheter, prostate, stones).
Assess: fluid balance, weight, JVP, BP, urine output, urinalysis, U&Es, creatinine; renal USS for obstruction.
Pre-renal AKI responds to fluid resuscitation; intrinsic/post-renal need specific treatment. Watch for hyperkalaemia, acidosis and fluid overload.
Prevent: adequate hydration, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACEi in dehydration, contrast), monitor high-risk patients.

drugs.name: IV crystalloid
drugs.notes: Balanced crystalloid boluses, reassess after each

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.when: Fluid overload with AKI (not for pre-renal oliguria)
drugs.notes: Does not treat AKI itself; avoid in hypovolaemia

drugs.name: Stop nephrotoxins
drugs.notes: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, aminoglycosides, contrast

drugs.name: Catheterisation
drugs.notes: Relieves post-renal AKI; monitor for post-obstructive diuresis

drugs.name: Treatment of hyperkalaemia
drugs.notes: Calcium gluconate, insulin+dextrose — see electrolytes

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-operative patient with urine output 0.2 mL/kg/h, tachycardic and hypotensive with dry mucous membranes.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Pre-renal AKI — IV fluid challenge and reassess; do not give diuretics.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Anuria after pelvic surgery.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Check the catheter (blockage) and do a renal USS for obstruction; assess renal function.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Rising creatinine with a nephrotoxic drug started recently.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Intrinsic AKI — stop the nephrotoxin (e.g. NSAID, aminoglycoside), monitor U&Es.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Enlarged prostate with chronic retention and renal impairment.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Post-renal AKI — catheterise urgently, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: AKI with K+ 6.8 and pulmonary oedema.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Refractory AKI with hyperkalaemia/overload — consider urgent dialysis; involve renal team.

keyValues: Cr rise ≥26.5 µmol/L in 48 h or 1.5× baseline
redFlags: Anuria — think obstruction, needs urgent renal USS + catheter.
Hyperkalaemia or severe acidosis in AKI — may need dialysis.
Pulmonary oedema from fluid overload — stop fluids, diurese.
management: Assess volume status; fluid challenge if hypovolaemic (pre-renal).
Catheterise to measure output accurately and exclude obstruction.
Stop nephrotoxins, treat the cause, monitor U&Es and output.
Escalate for dialysis if refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, or overload.
pitfalls: Do not give furosemide for oliguria from hypovolaemia — it worsens pre-renal AKI.
Anuria is not 'low output' — it suggests obstruction and needs urgent action.
A 'normal' creatinine can hide significant AKI in low-muscle-mass patients — use trends.

iv-fluids.name: Intravenous fluid prescription
iv-fluids.overview: IV fluids are drugs with indications, doses and harms. The exam tests assessing the patient's fluid status first, then choosing the right fluid and monitoring.
essentials: Prescribe IV fluids like a drug: assess fluid status (hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, overloaded), then choose fluid, rate and monitoring.
Crystalloids are first-line: balanced solutions (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) preferred over 0.9% saline (which can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis). Dextrose is for water replacement.
Maintenance: ~25-30 mL/kg/day water with Na+ and K+ (~1 mmol/kg/day each). Adjust for losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, drains, fever).
Resuscitation: rapid boluses (250-500 mL) for hypovolaemia/shock, reassess after each. Avoid over-resuscitation.
Monitor: fluid balance, weight, urine output, U&Es and clinical signs; reassess daily and stop when no longer needed.

drugs.name: Hartmann's / balanced crystalloid
drugs.notes: Closest to plasma; avoids hyperchloraemic acidosis

drugs.name: 0.9% sodium chloride
drugs.when: Resuscitation; when a balanced solution is unavailable; with blood products
drugs.notes: Large volumes cause hyperchloraemic acidosis

drugs.name: 5% dextrose
drugs.notes: Poor resuscitation fluid (distributes across all compartments)

drugs.name: Potassium chloride (in fluids)
drugs.notes: Add per renal function; max rates apply

drugs.name: 4% albumin / colloid
drugs.notes: Not routine for resuscitation

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Hypovolaemic patient needing resuscitation — which fluid first?
clinicalScenarios.answer: Balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's) boluses, reassessing after each.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Adult needing maintenance fluids.
clinicalScenarios.answer: ~25-30 mL/kg/day water with ~1 mmol/kg/day Na+ and K+; use a balanced solution.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient with heart failure becoming breathless after IV fluids.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Fluid overload — stop fluids, consider diuresis; reassess the plan and weight.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Large-volume paracentesis for ascites.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Give IV albumin alongside to prevent circulatory dysfunction.

redFlags: Signs of fluid overload (pulmonary oedema, raised JVP) — stop fluids, diurese.
Hypovolaemic shock — rapid resuscitation, not slow maintenance.
Heart or renal failure — fluids can worsen; be cautious and reassess.
management: Assess volume status; prescribe a clear plan (resuscitation vs maintenance vs replacement).
Choose balanced crystalloid; add K+ as needed (check renal function).
Monitor fluid balance, weight and U&Es; reassess daily.
Stop IV fluids as soon as the patient can drink.
pitfalls: Never prescribe '1 L over 24 h' for a shocked patient — resuscitation is bolus-based.
Large volumes of 0.9% saline cause hyperchloraemic acidosis — prefer balanced solutions.
Always reassess after each bolus rather than following a fixed prescription.

gi-bleeds.name: Gastrointestinal bleeds
gi-bleeds.overview: A major GI bleed is a resuscitation first, diagnosis second. The exam tests recognising the severity, resuscitating, and differentiating upper (variceal) from lower bleeding.
essentials: Upper GI bleed (haematemesis, melaena): peptic ulcer, varices (cirrhosis), Mallory-Weiss tear, gastritis. Lower GI bleed (fresh PR): diverticular, angiodysplasia, colorectal cancer, haemorrhoids.
Assess severity: haemodynamic status, Hb drop, shock. Melaena + compromise = significant upper GI bleed.
Resuscitate first: 2 large-bore IVs, bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, crossmatch), fluids/blood, correct coagulopathy. Consider tranexamic acid.
Upper GI: urgent endoscopy (within 24 h; within 1 h for variceal/severe). Variceal bleed: terlipressin + antibiotics + endoscopic banding.
Risk scores (Glasgow-Blatchford, Rockall) guide admission and endoscopy timing; re-bleeding escalates to repeat endoscopy/IR/surgery.

drugs.name: Terlipressin
drugs.notes: IV; reduces portal pressure; watch for ischaemia/hyponatraemia

drugs.name: Prophylactic antibiotics
drugs.when: Variceal bleed / cirrhosis with GI bleed
drugs.notes: Reduces mortality and re-bleeding; per local policy

drugs.name: Proton pump inhibitor (IV)
drugs.when: Non-variceal upper GI bleed / after endoscopic therapy
drugs.notes: IV omeprazole/esomeprazole

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.notes: Consider early; per local policy

drugs.name: Blood products
drugs.notes: Restrictive transfusion (Hb <70-80 g/L) unless cardiac

drugs.name: Vitamin K / PCC
drugs.notes: Reverse if bleeding

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Cirrhotic patient with haematemesis, tachycardic and hypotensive.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Variceal bleed — resuscitate, terlipressin + antibiotics, urgent endoscopy for banding.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Melaena with haemodynamic compromise.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Significant upper GI bleed — IV access, bloods/crossmatch, fluids/blood, then urgent endoscopy.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient on warfarin with a GI bleed and INR 4.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Reverse with IV vitamin K + PCC while resuscitating; urgent endoscopy.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fresh PR bleeding in a stable 55-year-old.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Lower GI bleed — resuscitate, identify source (colonoscopy/CT), treat the cause.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Re-bleeding after endoscopic therapy.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Escalate — repeat endoscopy, consider IR embolisation or surgery.

redFlags: Haematemesis with shock — massive bleed, resuscitate aggressively.
Variceal bleed in cirrhosis — high mortality, terlipressin + antibiotics urgently.
Re-bleeding after endoscopy — escalate.
management: ABC, two large-bore IVs, bloods + crossmatch, fluids/blood, correct coagulopathy.
Upper GI: urgent endoscopy; variceal → terlipressin + antibiotics + banding.
Lower GI: resuscitate, identify source (colonoscopy/CT), treat the cause.
Monitor Hb and haemodynamics; repeat endoscopy if re-bleeding.
pitfalls: Do not scope an unstable patient — resuscitate first.
A normal Hb early in a bleed is misleading — it falls with fluid resuscitation.
In cirrhosis, always consider variceal bleeding and give antibiotics — not just a PPI.

hepatic-encephalopathy.name: Hepatic encephalopathy
hepatic-encephalopathy.overview: A neuropsychiatric syndrome of liver failure driven by ammonia and other toxins. The exam tests finding the precipitants — treating them is the priority.
essentials: Neuropsychiatric syndrome in liver failure due to accumulation of ammonia and other toxins (impaired hepatic clearance).
Precipitants: GI bleed, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, dehydration, high protein load, portosystemic shunting.
Grading (West Haven): I mild confusion/altered sleep, II lethargy/disorientation, III somnolent but rousable, IV coma.
Clinical: altered consciousness, asterixis (flapping tremor), confusion, personality change, fetor hepaticus.
Exclude other causes of confusion (hypoglycaemia, sepsis, intracranial bleed, Wernicke's) — never assume HH is the whole story.

drugs.name: Lactulose
drugs.notes: Oral/enema; titrate to 2-3 soft stools/day; reduces ammonia via the gut

drugs.name: Rifaximin
drugs.notes: Non-absorbed antibiotic reducing ammonia-producing gut flora

drugs.name: Avoid sedatives
drugs.notes: Benzodiazepines/opiates worsen it

drugs.name: Treat the precipitant
drugs.notes: Antibiotics for SBP, terlipressin for varices, correct electrolytes

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Cirrhotic patient becomes confused and asterixic after a GI bleed.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by the bleed — lactulose + treat the bleed (terlipressin, antibiotics, banding).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Grade IV encephalopathy (coma) in liver failure.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Airway protection, ICU, lactulose/rifaximin, treat the precipitant; consider liver unit transfer.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: New confusion in cirrhosis with no obvious cause.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Screen for precipitants — infection (SBP), GI bleed, constipation, electrolytes, drugs.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Confusion in a malnourished alcoholic patient.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider Wernicke's encephalopathy — give parenteral thiamine before glucose; also check for other causes.

redFlags: Grade III-IV encephalopathy — airway protection, ICU.
New confusion in cirrhosis — always exclude GI bleed, sepsis and hypoglycaemia.
Deterioration despite treatment — re-evaluate for precipitants.
management: Treat the precipitant (bleed, infection, constipation, electrolytes).
Lactulose (oral/enema); add rifaximin if recurrent.
Correct electrolytes, avoid sedatives and a high protein load acutely.
Exclude other causes of altered consciousness.
pitfalls: Never sedate a confused cirrhotic patient — it worsens encephalopathy.
Encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion — always look for a precipitant.
Give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients (Wernicke's).

ascites.name: Ascites
ascites.overview: Ascites usually reflects portal hypertension (cirrhosis). The exam tests diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, SBP) and the diuretic/paracentesis strategy.
essentials: Ascites = peritoneal fluid accumulation. Most commonly portal hypertension (cirrhosis); other causes: malignancy, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, TB, pancreatitis.
Diagnosis: clinical (shifting dullness, fluid thrill), USS, diagnostic paracentesis.
SAAG (serum-ascites albumin gradient): ≥11 g/L indicates portal hypertension; <11 g/L suggests another cause (malignancy, TB, pancreatitis).
Cirrhotic ascites: sodium restriction, spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) ± furosemide. Large-volume paracentesis with albumin for tense ascites.
Complications: SBP (fever, abdominal pain, rising WCC), refractory ascites, hepatorenal syndrome.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.notes: Start 100 mg; titrate; watch for hyperkalaemia and renal impairment

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.notes: Usually 40 mg; monitor U&Es and weight

drugs.name: IV albumin
drugs.notes: Prevents circulatory dysfunction; 20% albumin

drugs.name: IV antibiotics (cefotaxime)
drugs.notes: With albumin; per local policy

drugs.name: Vasoconstrictors (terlipressin)
drugs.notes: With albumin; specialist use

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Cirrhotic patient with ascites develops fever and abdominal pain; ascitic neutrophils 400/mm3.
clinicalScenarios.answer: SBP — IV cefotaxime + albumin; secondary prophylaxis afterwards.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Tense ascites causing respiratory compromise.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Large-volume paracentesis with IV albumin.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: New ascites in a patient with known malignancy.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider malignant ascites — diagnostic paracentesis with cytology; SAAG <11 g/L.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Cirrhotic ascites not responding to spironolactone/furosemide.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Refractory ascites — consider regular paracentesis, TIPS assessment, or transplant referral.

redFlags: Fever/abdominal pain with ascites — SBP, urgent paracentesis + antibiotics.
Rising creatinine with ascites — hepatorenal syndrome.
Tense ascites with respiratory compromise — therapeutic paracentesis + albumin.
management: Diagnostic paracentesis: SAAG, cell count, culture, albumin.
Cirrhotic ascites: sodium restriction, spironolactone ± furosemide.
Tense ascites: large-volume paracentesis with IV albumin.
SBP: IV antibiotics + albumin; treat the underlying liver disease.
pitfalls: Always do a diagnostic paracentesis — SBP can be subtle and is easily missed.
Do not drain large volumes without albumin — risk of circulatory collapse.
Ascites in cirrhosis is not 'just third-spacing' — it signals advanced disease and complications.

jaundice.name: Jaundice
jaundice.overview: Jaundice is classified pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic, and the pattern of LFTs points to the cause. The exam tests spotting obstructive jaundice and the cholangitis emergency.
essentials: Jaundice = yellow discolouration from hyperbilirubinaemia. Classify: pre-hepatic (haemolysis — unconjugated), hepatic (hepatocellular — mixed), post-hepatic (obstructive — conjugated).
Pre-hepatic: haemolysis (raised unconjugated bilirubin, normal LFTs, reticulocytosis).
Hepatic: viral hepatitis, alcohol, drugs, autoimmune, cirrhosis — raised transaminases (ALT/AST).
Post-hepatic/obstructive: gallstones, malignancy (pancreatic head), stricture — raised ALP/GGT, conjugated bilirubin, pale stools, dark urine.
Investigations: LFTs, bilirubin (total/conjugated), FBC, USS (biliary dilatation), viral serology, autoimmune screen.

drugs.name: IV antibiotics
drugs.notes: Broad-spectrum per local policy; then urgent biliary drainage

drugs.name: Vitamin K
drugs.notes: Fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption — correct before procedures

drugs.name: Analgesia (avoid hepatotoxic)
drugs.notes: NSAIDs/paracetamol per liver function; avoid opioids that worsen spasm (pethidine debated)

drugs.name: Ursodeoxycholic acid
drugs.notes: Specialist; e.g. primary biliary cholangitis

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Jaundice with pale stools, dark urine, raised ALP/GGT and dilated ducts on USS.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Obstructive jaundice — find the cause (gallstone/malignancy); may need ERCP or drainage.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (Charcot's triad).
clinicalScenarios.answer: Cholangitis — IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Painless jaundice in an elderly patient with weight loss.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Suspect pancreatic (head) malignancy — urgent imaging (CT/USS) and referral.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Jaundice with very high ALT after starting a new drug.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Hepatocellular (drug-induced) jaundice — stop the culprit, check viral/autoimmune causes.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a normal blood film otherwise well.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider Gilbert's syndrome (benign) or haemolysis — check LFTs and haemolysis screen.

redFlags: Cholangitis — IV antibiotics + urgent biliary drainage (ERCP).
Acute liver failure (coagulopathy, encephalopathy) — urgent hepatology/ICU.
Painless jaundice in the elderly — think pancreatic malignancy.
management: Classify the type of jaundice (pre-hepatic/hepatic/post-hepatic).
LFTs, bilirubin, FBC, USS; further tests by suspected cause.
Obstructive: treat the cause (ERCP for stones, drainage for malignancy).
Cholangitis: IV antibiotics, urgent biliary drainage.
pitfalls: Always check conjugated vs unconjugated bilirubin — it directs the classification.
Charcot's triad may be incomplete — a fever with obstructive jaundice is still cholangitis until proven otherwise.
Do not overlook drug-induced liver injury — take a full drug history.

neutropenic-sepsis.name: Neutropenic sepsis
neutropenic-sepsis.overview: A haematological emergency where the usual signs of infection may be absent. The exam tests the rule: any fever in a neutropenic patient is sepsis until proven otherwise, and antibiotics must not wait.
essentials: Neutropenic sepsis = temperature ≥38°C (or sepsis signs) with neutrophils <0.5 × 10^9/L, in a patient on chemotherapy or with haematological malignancy. A medical emergency.
Neutropenic patients mount no inflammatory response — they may look deceptively well with minimal signs.
Immediate management (within 1 hour): blood cultures, FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, lactate, then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics — do not wait for results.
Look for a source: line infection, chest, urine, skin, perianal. Consider antifungal if fever persists despite antibiotics.
Monitor temperature, observations, cultures and response; escalate if deteriorating.

drugs.name: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
drugs.notes: Piperacillin-tazobactam (or per local policy); within 1 hour

drugs.name: Antifungal (e.g. amphotericin/caspofungin)
drugs.when: Persistent fever after 48-72 h of antibiotics
drugs.notes: Covers fungal infection; specialist input

drugs.name: G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor)
drugs.notes: Stimulates neutrophil recovery

drugs.name: IV fluids
drugs.notes: Part of Sepsis Six resuscitation

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Chemotherapy patient, temperature 38.5°C, neutrophils 0.3.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Neutropenic sepsis — blood cultures then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Neutropenic patient with a central line and fever.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider line sepsis — cultures (peripheral + line), antibiotics, consider line removal.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fever persists after 72 h of appropriate antibiotics.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider fungal infection — add antifungal; re-image and re-culture.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Neutropenic patient with hypotension and lactate 3.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Septic shock — Sepsis Six, aggressive fluids, early senior/ICU involvement.

redFlags: Any fever in a neutropenic patient — treat as sepsis immediately.
Hypotension/shock — aggressive resuscitation + antibiotics.
Persistent fever despite 48-72 h of antibiotics — consider fungal infection.
management: Sepsis Six + blood cultures, FBC, lactate, then IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
Look for and treat the source (line, chest, urine, skin).
Monitor response; add antifungal if fever persists.
Involve the haematology/oncology team early.
pitfalls: A well-looking neutropenic patient can be profoundly septic — do not be reassured.
Never delay antibiotics to wait for cultures or imaging.
Remember line sepsis as a source — examine the central line site.

congenital-bleeding.name: Congenital bleeding disorders
congenital-bleeding.overview: Haemophilia and von Willebrand disease present with bleeding into joints/muscles or mucocutaneous bleeding. The exam tests recognising the pattern and replacing the missing factor.
essentials: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and B (factor IX deficiency): X-linked, bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) and muscles; severity by factor level.
von Willebrand disease: the most common inherited bleeding disorder — mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising), prolonged bleeding time, low vWF.
Acute bleeding in haemophilia: replace the missing factor urgently. Avoid IM injections, aspirin and NSAIDs.
Haemarthrosis: factor replacement + analgesia + rest; avoid joint aspiration unless tense.
Carriers/affected patients need specialist haematology input for surgery, dental work and major bleeding.

drugs.name: Factor VIII concentrate
drugs.notes: Urgent replacement; dose by severity/weight

drugs.name: Factor IX concentrate
drugs.notes: Urgent replacement

drugs.name: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
drugs.when: Mild haemophilia A / mild von Willebrand disease
drugs.notes: Releases stored factor VIII/vWF; not for severe disease

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.notes: Antifibrinolytic; adjunct

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid / von Willebrand factor concentrate
drugs.notes: vWF-containing factor concentrate for severe bleeding

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Known haemophilia A with a swollen, painful knee after minor trauma.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Haemarthrosis — factor VIII replacement + analgesia + rest (avoid aspirin/NSAIDs).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Haemophiliac with a head injury after a fall.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Urgent factor replacement and imaging — intracranial bleed is life-threatening.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Young woman with heavy periods, easy bruising and epistaxis; prolonged bleeding time.
clinicalScenarios.answer: von Willebrand disease — check vWF antigen/activity; desmopressin or vWF concentrate for bleeding.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient with vWD needing a dental extraction.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Plan with haematology — tranexamic acid ± desmopressin/factor cover.

redFlags: Major bleeding or head injury in a haemophiliac — urgent factor replacement.
Intracranial bleed — factor replacement + urgent imaging.
Bleeding not controlled by factor — consider inhibitors.
management: Acute bleed: replace the deficient factor urgently.
Haemarthrosis: factor + analgesia + rest; avoid aspiration.
Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs/IM injections.
Involve haematology for all significant bleeds and procedures.
pitfalls: Do not give IM injections or NSAIDs in haemophilia.
Desmopressin works only in mild haemophilia A and mild vWD — not severe disease.
Always consider an intracranial bleed after head injury in a bleeding disorder.

spinal-cord-compression.name: Spinal cord compression
spinal-cord-compression.overview: An oncological emergency where outcome depends on how early you act. The exam tests recognising the red flags and starting dexamethasone before imaging.
essentials: Malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC): cord/cauda equina compression by tumour (metastatic — prostate, breast, lung, myeloma).

Red flags: new back pain (especially thoracic), progressive neurological deficit, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction, gait disturbance. Back pain + neurological symptoms in a cancer patient = MSCC until proven otherwise.
Immediate: high-dose dexamethasone (reduces oedema), urgent MRI whole spine (within 24 h), oncology/neurosurgery referral.
Do not delay treatment for the diagnosis — treat empirically if suspicion is high.
Outcome depends on pre-treatment neurological status — early recognition is critical.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.notes: High-dose (e.g. 16 mg/day) with gastric protection; reduces cord oedema

drugs.name: Analgesia
drugs.notes: Regular paracetamol/opioid; avoid NSAIDs if thrombocytopenia

drugs.name: LMWH
drugs.notes: Immobility risk

drugs.name: Bisphosphonate / denosumab
drugs.notes: Reduces skeletal events

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient with metastatic prostate cancer develops new thoracic back pain and leg weakness.
clinicalScenarios.answer: MSCC — high-dose dexamethasone + urgent MRI whole spine (within 24 h), oncology/neurosurgery referral.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Cancer patient with saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Cauda equina syndrome — emergency MRI and urgent surgical referral.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Known lung cancer with a sensory level and gait disturbance.
clinicalScenarios.answer: MSCC — dexamethasone, urgent MRI, radiotherapy/surgery per team.

keyValues: Back pain + neuro deficit, sensory level, sphincter dysfunction
redFlags: Back pain + any neurological symptom in a cancer patient — MSCC until proven otherwise.
Sensory level, leg weakness, or bladder/bowel dysfunction — emergency.
Cauda equina (saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention) — surgical emergency.
management: High-dose dexamethasone immediately.
Urgent MRI whole spine (within 24 h).
Oncology/neurosurgery referral; treat the primary malignancy.
Analgesia, log-roll care, monitor neurology.
pitfalls: Do not wait for imaging to start dexamethasone if suspicion is high.
A normal plain X-ray does not exclude MSCC — it needs MRI.
Bladder/bowel dysfunction is a late sign — act on back pain + neurology earlier.

diabetes-control.name: Diabetes control
diabetes-control.overview: Diabetic emergencies (DKA, HHS) and inpatient glycaemic control are heavily examined. The exam tests safe management — especially potassium handling in DKA.
essentials: Type 1 (insulin deficiency, autoimmune) vs type 2 (insulin resistance + relative deficiency). Acute complications: DKA, HHS, hypoglycaemia.
DKA (type 1): hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia + acidosis. Precipitants: infection, missed insulin, MI, stress. Treat: IV fluids, fixed-rate insulin infusion, potassium replacement, treat precipitant.
HHS (type 2): severe hyperglycaemia without significant ketosis/acidosis, marked dehydration. Treat: large-volume fluids, cautious insulin, correct electrolytes.
Inpatient glycaemic control: monitor glucose, basal-bolus insulin, avoid prolonged hypo/hyperglycaemia; involve the diabetes team.
Sick-day rules: never stop insulin in type 1, increase monitoring, seek help if vomiting/unwell.

drugs.name: Fixed-rate IV insulin
drugs.notes: 0.1 unit/kg/h (DKA); monitor glucose and K+ hourly

drugs.name: IV fluids (0.9% saline)
drugs.notes: Rapid initial resuscitation, then guided by status

drugs.name: Potassium replacement
drugs.notes: Insulin drives K+ down; replace before/with insulin if low

drugs.name: Basal-bolus insulin
drugs.notes: Long-acting basal + short-acting mealtime doses

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.notes: Hold in acute illness/contrast (lactic acidosis risk)

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Type 1 diabetes with DKA and K+ 3.2.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Replace potassium before/with insulin — insulin shifts K+ intracellularly and can cause dangerous hypokalaemia.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Type 2 diabetes, glucose 38 mmol/L, marked dehydration, no significant ketosis.
clinicalScenarios.answer: HHS — aggressive fluids, cautious insulin, correct electrolytes.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Type 1 diabetic vomiting with high glucose and ketones.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Sick-day rules — never stop insulin, monitor glucose/ketones, seek help; treat as DKA if severe.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Inpatient with erratic glucose on the ward.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Basal-bolus insulin regimen + monitor + diabetes team input.

keyValues: Glucose often >30 mmol/L, no significant ketosis
IV fluids, fixed-rate insulin, K+ replacement
redFlags: DKA with K+ <3.5 — replace K+ before insulin.
HHS with severe dehydration — large-volume fluid resuscitation.
Recurrent hypoglycaemia — review the insulin regimen.
management: DKA: fluids, fixed-rate insulin, K+ replacement, treat precipitant, monitor glucose/ketones/K+.
HHS: aggressive fluids, cautious insulin, correct electrolytes.
Inpatient: basal-bolus insulin, monitor glucose, diabetes team input.
Educate on sick-day rules and never stopping insulin in type 1.
pitfalls: Insulin without potassium replacement in DKA can cause fatal hypokalaemia.
HHS needs much larger fluid volumes than DKA.
Do not stop a type 1 diabetic's insulin because they are 'not eating'.

hypoglycaemia.name: Hypoglycaemia
hypoglycaemia.overview: A common inpatient emergency where the treatment depends on whether the patient can swallow. The exam tests the conscious vs unconscious pathway.
essentials: Hypoglycaemia = glucose <4.0 mmol/L (in diabetics) with symptoms. Causes: excess insulin/oral hypoglycaemics, missed meals, exercise, alcohol, sepsis, renal/hepatic failure.
Symptoms: autonomic (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) and neuroglycopenic (confusion, drowsiness, seizures, coma).
Treatment: if conscious and able to swallow → oral fast-acting carbohydrate, then long-acting starchy food. If unconscious/unable → IV glucose (10%) or IM glucagon.
Recheck glucose 10-15 min after treatment; repeat if still low; identify and treat the cause.
Inpatients: review the insulin regimen, monitor glucose, involve the diabetes team.

drugs.name: Oral glucose (glucose tablets/sugary drink)
drugs.notes: Follow with long-acting carbohydrate

drugs.name: IV glucose 10%
drugs.notes: 100-200 mL bolus, then monitor; protect the airway

drugs.name: IM glucagon
drugs.notes: 1 mg IM; works only with stored glycogen (less effective in alcohol/fasting)

drugs.name: Long-acting carbohydrate
drugs.notes: Prevents recurrence (e.g. toast, biscuit)

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Diabetic found unconscious with glucose 1.8 mmol/L.
clinicalScenarios.answer: IV 10% glucose (or IM glucagon) with airway protection; recheck 10-15 min later.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Diabetic patient conscious with a glucose of 3.2 after a missed meal.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Oral fast-acting carbohydrate then long-acting starchy food; review the regimen.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Non-diabetic patient with recurrent hypoglycaemia.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Investigate — insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency, sepsis, alcohol; check insulin/C-peptide levels.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Recurrent hypoglycaemia in a hospital patient on insulin.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Review the insulin dose and regimen; consider causes and involve the diabetes team.

redFlags: Unconscious/seizing — IV glucose/glucagon, protect the airway.
Recurrent hypoglycaemia — review medication and look for the cause.
Hypoglycaemia in a non-diabetic — investigate (insulinoma, adrenal, sepsis).
management: Conscious: oral glucose, then long-acting carbohydrate.
Unconscious: IV 10% glucose or IM glucagon, recheck.
Identify and treat the cause (insulin dose, missed meal, sepsis).
Review and adjust the diabetes regimen; involve the diabetes team.
pitfalls: Oral treatment for an unconscious patient risks aspiration — use IV glucose/glucagon.
Glucagon is less effective in alcohol-related or prolonged fasting hypoglycaemia (low glycogen).
Always recheck glucose — a single treatment may not be enough.

diabetic-foot.name: Diabetic foot complications + sepsis
diabetic-foot.overview: A common and dangerous problem where neuropathy, ischaemia and infection combine. The exam tests recognising the infected foot and escalating to surgery.
essentials: Diabetic foot disease = neuropathy (loss of protective sensation) + ischaemia (PAD) + infection. Ulcers are often painless and on pressure points.
Assess: neurovascular status (monofilament, pulses, ABPI), ulcer depth, signs of infection (erythema, discharge, odour, crepitus), systemic sepsis.
Infected diabetic foot is a surgical emergency — deep infection, osteomyelitis and gangrene progress rapidly. IV antibiotics + urgent surgical debridement.
Classify severity (Wagner / IDSA / IWGDF) to guide management; osteomyelitis via probe-to-bone, MRI, prolonged antibiotics.
Prevention: foot examination at every diabetes review, podiatry, offloading, glycaemic control, smoking cessation.

drugs.name: IV antibiotics
drugs.notes: Broad-spectrum per local policy; guided by wound swabs

drugs.name: Analgesia
drugs.notes: Regular; neuropathy may mask pain

drugs.name: Antiplatelet + statin
drugs.notes: Secondary prevention

drugs.name: Insulin optimisation
drugs.notes: Aids wound healing

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Diabetic foot ulcer with crepitus, spreading infection and fever.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Necrotising infection — IV antibiotics + urgent surgical debridement.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Deep ulcer with positive probe-to-bone.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Suspect osteomyelitis — MRI, prolonged antibiotics, consider amputation.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Painless plantar ulcer with loss of monofilament sensation.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Neuropathic ulcer — offloading, podiatry, glycaemic control, foot care.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Diabetic with rest pain and an ABPI of 0.4.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Ischaemic component — vascular review for revascularisation; best medical therapy.

keyValues: Assess ischaemia (calcified vessels may over-read in diabetes)
redFlags: Systemic sepsis from a diabetic foot — emergency, IV antibiotics + surgery.
Crepitus, gas on X-ray — necrotising infection, urgent debridement.
Deep ulcer with exposed bone — osteomyelitis.
management: Assess neurovascular status and ulcer characteristics.
Infected: wound swab, IV antibiotics, urgent surgical debridement.
Osteomyelitis: MRI, prolonged antibiotics, consider amputation.
Prevention: podiatry, offloading, glycaemic control, smoking cessation.
pitfalls: A painless foot ulcer is not benign — neuropathy hides severe infection.
An ABPI >1.3 in diabetes is falsely reassuring (calcified vessels).
Never delay surgery in a foot with spreading infection or gas.

acute-confusional-states.name: Acute confusional states
acute-confusional-states.overview: Delirium is common, serious and usually reversible. The exam tests recognising it, hunting for the cause (PINCH ME), and avoiding sedation.
essentials: Delirium = acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness/attention, common in the elderly and acutely ill. Distinguish from dementia (chronic, progressive) and psychiatric illness.
Causes (PINCH ME / DIMS): infection, drugs, metabolic (electrolytes, glucose, hypoxia), constipation, urinary retention, pain, dehydration, sensory impairment, sleep deprivation.
Assess: history (onset, fluctuation), cognitive testing (AMT4/6-CIT), observations, bloods (FBC, U&E, glucose, LFT, TFT, CRP), urine, ECG, sepsis screen.
Management: treat the underlying cause, non-pharmacological measures first (reorientation, family, sensory aids, mobilisation, sleep), avoid sedatives.
Prevent: early mobilisation, hydration, avoid unnecessary catheters/drugs, good sleep hygiene.

drugs.name: Treat the cause (antibiotics etc.)
drugs.notes: Infection, dehydration, constipation, retention are common

drugs.name: Haloperidol (cautious)
drugs.when: Severe distress/risk not controlled by non-drug measures
drugs.notes: Low dose; avoid in Parkinson's/dementia with Lewy bodies (use quetiapine); ECG monitoring

drugs.name: Avoid benzodiazepines
drugs.notes: Worsen delirium; except in alcohol withdrawal

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Elderly patient with acute fluctuating confusion and inattention.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Delirium — hunt for the cause (PINCH ME); treat the underlying problem.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Confused patient with a raised WCC and fever.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Delirium from infection — treat sepsis, reorient, avoid sedation.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Confused elderly patient with a palpable bladder.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Urinary retention — catheterise; retention is a common reversible cause of delirium.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Agitated delirious patient at risk of falling.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Non-pharmacological measures first; use a low-dose antipsychotic only if severe distress/risk persists.

keyValues: Infection, drugs, metabolic, constipation, retention, pain
Age, date of birth, place, year
redFlags: New confusion + fever — sepsis, treat urgently.
Hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, or hypotension causing confusion — correct immediately.
Focal neurology or head injury — consider intracranial bleed.
management: Screen for and treat the underlying cause (PINCH ME).
Non-pharmacological measures first (reorientation, family, sensory aids).
Avoid sedatives; use cautiously only for severe distress/risk.
Prevent: mobilisation, hydration, avoid catheters, good sleep.
pitfalls: Delirium is a symptom — always find and treat the cause.
Do not sedate a delirious patient as a first response.
Avoid antipsychotics in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.

falls-elderly.name: Falls in elderly persons
falls-elderly.overview: Falls are multifactorial and often a marker of serious underlying disease. The exam tests the causes (including cardiac and drug-related) and the injury/complication screen.
essentials: Falls in the elderly are multifactorial: intrinsic (postural hypotension, gait/balance, visual, cognitive, medication, cardiac syncope) + extrinsic (environmental hazards).
