Assess the cause: circumstances, loss of consciousness, prodrome, medications (antihypertensives, sedatives), mobility, vision, cognition, cardiac causes.
Examine for injury: head injury, fracture (hip, wrist, pelvis), soft tissue. Check for 'long lie' (rhabdomyolysis, hypothermia, pressure injury).
Investigations: FBC, U&E, glucose, ECG, lying/standing BP; cardiac monitoring if syncope suspected.
Prevention: multifactorial intervention — medication review, strength/balance exercise, vision, home hazard reduction, treat postural hypotension.

drugs.name: Review culprit drugs
drugs.notes: Antihypertensives, sedatives, anticholinergics, hypoglycaemics

drugs.name: Analgesia
drugs.notes: Regular; avoid over-sedation

drugs.name: Calcium/vitamin D
drugs.notes: Bone health; assess fracture risk (FRAX)

drugs.name: Treatment of postural hypotension
drugs.notes: Fludrocortisone/midodrine (specialist) + lifestyle measures

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Elderly patient found on the floor several hours later.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Look for 'long lie' complications — rhabdomyolysis, hypothermia, pressure injury; check CK and renal function.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Elderly patient on an antihypertensive with recurrent falls and a 25 mmHg BP drop on standing.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Postural hypotension — review the drug, hydration, and lying/standing BP.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fall with a head injury in a patient on anticoagulation.
clinicalScenarios.answer: CT head and reverse anticoagulation — high risk of intracranial bleed.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fall with hip pain and inability to weight-bear.
clinicalScenarios.answer: X-ray to exclude hip fracture; analgesia and orthopaedic referral.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Recurrent unexplained falls with no prodrome.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider cardiac cause (arrhythmia) — ECG and cardiac monitoring.

keyValues: >1 h on floor — rhabdo, hypothermia, pressure injury
Medication review, exercise, vision, home safety
redFlags: Fall with head injury on anticoagulation — CT head, reverse anticoagulation.
Fall with hip pain/inability to weight-bear — X-ray, exclude fracture.
Recurrent falls or syncope — cardiac assessment.
management: Assess and treat any injury (fracture, head injury).
Identify the cause (postural hypotension, medication, cardiac, gait).
Multifactorial prevention: medication review, exercise, vision, home safety.
Check for long-lie complications.
pitfalls: Always check lying/standing BP — postural hypotension is a common, treatable cause.
Do not dismiss a fall as 'mechanical' — look for syncope and cardiac causes.
In the elderly, a fall may be the presenting sign of sepsis, MI or a new medication effect.

obs-gynae-emergencies.name: Gynaecology and Obstetric emergencies
obs-gynae-emergencies.overview: Bleeding in pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy and postpartum haemorrhage are the key emergencies. The exam tests thinking of pregnancy in any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain.
essentials: Ectopic pregnancy: pregnancy + abdominal pain/bleeding/collapse. Ruptured ectopic is a surgical emergency (haemorrhagic shock). Always do a pregnancy test in any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain.
Miscarriage: vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy — threatened, inevitable, missed, complete. USS confirms; manage expectantly/medically/surgically (ERPC).
Antepartum haemorrhage (APH): bleeding after 24 weeks — placenta praevia (painless) vs placental abruption (painful, rigid uterus, fetal distress). Both emergencies.
Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH): >500 mL (vaginal) or >1000 mL (CS). Treat: call for help, IV access, fluids/blood, uterotonics, identify cause (4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin).
Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia: hypertension + proteinuria after 20 weeks; headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain are red flags.

drugs.name: Oxytocin
drugs.notes: IV/IM; also used for induction/augmentation

drugs.name: Ergometrine
drugs.notes: Contraindicated in hypertension/pre-eclampsia

drugs.name: Carboprost (prostaglandin)
drugs.notes: Contraindicated in asthma

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.notes: IV; prevents/treats seizures; monitor reflexes and respiratory rate

drugs.name: Antihypertensives (labetalol/nifedipine)
drugs.notes: Control BP; hydralazine IV in crisis

drugs.name: Anti-D immunoglobulin
drugs.notes: Prevents haemolytic disease of the newborn

drugs.name: Methotrexate
drugs.notes: Specialist; not for ruptured ectopic

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain, PV bleeding and collapse.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy — pregnancy test, resuscitate, urgent gynae/surgery.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: PPH of 1200 mL after delivery.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Call for help, IV access, fluids/blood, oxytocin, identify the cause (4 Ts).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Painless PV bleeding at 34 weeks with placenta praevia on USS.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Antepartum haemorrhage — admit, monitor mother and fetus, plan delivery; avoid PV examination.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Painful bleeding with a rigid uterus and fetal distress.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Placental abruption — emergency, resuscitate and arrange urgent delivery.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 34-week pregnant patient with headache, visual disturbance and BP 170/110.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Severe pre-eclampsia — control BP, magnesium sulfate, urgent obstetric review/delivery.

redFlags: Ruptured ectopic (collapse, shoulder-tip pain) — immediate surgery.
Placental abruption (painful, rigid abdomen, fetal distress) — emergency delivery.
Eclampsia (seizures) — magnesium sulfate, control BP, urgent delivery.
management: Always pregnancy-test women of reproductive age with abdominal pain.
Ectopic: IV access, crossmatch, urgent gynae/surgery.
PPH: call for help, fluids/blood, uterotonics, massage, treat the cause.
Pre-eclampsia: monitor BP, magnesium for eclampsia, control BP, deliver.
pitfalls: Never miss an ectopic — always check a pregnancy test.
Do not perform a PV examination in suspected placenta praevia.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension/pre-eclampsia.

skin-rashes.name: Skin rashes in the acute setting
skin-rashes.overview: Most rashes are benign, but a few are emergencies. The exam tests recognising the life-threatening rashes first (meningococcal, SJS/TEN, necrotising fasciitis).
essentials: Identify life-threatening rashes first: meningococcal septicaemia (non-blanching purpura, fever, ill), SJS/TEN (blistering, mucosal involvement, drug-induced), necrotising fasciitis (severe pain, rapidly spreading), anaphylaxis (urticaria + systemic).
Non-blanching purpura + fever = meningococcal until proven otherwise — IV antibiotics immediately.
Common rashes: urticaria (allergic, itchy, blanch), cellulitis (erythema, warmth, pain, fever), shingles (vesicular, dermatomal, painful), scabies (itchy, burrows), drug eruptions.
Assess: distribution, morphology (macule, papule, vesicle, bulla, purpura), mucosal involvement, systemic symptoms, drug history.
Cellulitis: IV/oral antibiotics, mark the edge, monitor. Erysipelas: superficial, well-demarcated.

drugs.name: IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone)
drugs.notes: Immediately — do not wait for confirmation

drugs.name: Antihistamines
drugs.notes: Symptomatic; remove the trigger

drugs.name: Antibiotics (flucloxacillin/penicillin)
drugs.notes: Per local policy; mark the edge and monitor

drugs.name: Aciclovir
drugs.notes: Antiviral; analgesia important

drugs.name: Stop the culprit drug
drugs.notes: Immediate drug withdrawal is the key step

drugs.name: Adrenaline (IM)
drugs.notes: 500 mcg IM; first-line

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Febrile, unwell child with a non-blanching purpuric rash.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Meningococcal sepsis — IV antibiotics immediately.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient on a new drug with widespread blistering and oral mucosal involvement.
clinicalScenarios.answer: SJS/TEN — stop the culprit drug and seek urgent specialist care.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Rapidly spreading painful erythema with crepitus.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Necrotising fasciitis — urgent surgical debridement + IV antibiotics.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Unilateral painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Shingles — aciclovir (± within 72 h) and analgesia.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Well patient with itchy blanching wheals after a new food.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Urticaria — antihistamines, remove the trigger; treat anaphylaxis if systemic.

redFlags: Non-blanching rash + fever/illness — meningococcal, treat immediately.
Rapidly spreading painful erythema — necrotising fasciitis.
Blistering + mucosal involvement — SJS/TEN, stop the culprit drug.
management: ABC; treat life-threatening rashes immediately (meningococcal antibiotics).
Cellulitis: antibiotics, mark the edge, monitor response.
Urticaria: antihistamines, remove the trigger, treat anaphylaxis if systemic.
Identify and stop culprit drugs in drug eruptions.
pitfalls: A non-blanching rash in a febrile patient is an emergency — act before the diagnosis is confirmed.
Do not miss mucosal involvement in a blistering rash — it suggests SJS/TEN.
Always take a drug history — many acute rashes are drug-induced.

febrile-patient.name: The febrile patient
febrile-patient.overview: Fever plus organ dysfunction is sepsis, and sepsis is time-critical. The exam tests the Sepsis Six and finding the source within the first hour.
essentials: Fever = temperature ≥38°C. Assess for sepsis (infection + organ dysfunction) using NEWS2 and clinical judgement. Sepsis is time-critical — treat within 1 hour.
Sepsis Six: oxygen, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, urine output. Give antibiotics within 1 hour of suspected sepsis.
Find the source: respiratory (cough, sputum, chest signs), urinary (dysuria, loin pain), skin/soft tissue, line, abdominal, CNS (meningitis), endocarditis.
Risk factors for poor outcome: elderly, immunocompromised (neutropenia, steroids, HIV), malignancy, diabetes, pregnancy, indwelling devices.
Monitor: observations (NEWS2), lactate, cultures, response to antibiotics. Escalate if deteriorating or not improving.

drugs.name: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
drugs.notes: Per local policy; do not delay for cultures

drugs.name: IV crystalloid
drugs.notes: Fluid boluses, reassess; noradrenaline if MAP <65

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.when: Hypoxia / as part of Sepsis Six
drugs.notes: Target 94-98% (88-92% if hypercapnia risk)

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.notes: Does not treat the cause; avoid masking deterioration

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Temperature 38.5°C, NEWS2 6, lactate 3.5.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Suspected sepsis — Sepsis Six within 1 hour (cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids, oxygen, lactate, urine output).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fever with cough, sputum and focal chest signs.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Pneumonia — assess severity (CURB-65), antibiotics, oxygen; find the organism where possible.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fever with dysuria and loin pain.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Pyelonephritis/UTI — urine culture, antibiotics; consider obstruction with USS if not improving.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fever in a patient with a central line.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider line sepsis — cultures (peripheral + line), antibiotics, consider line removal.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fever with neck stiffness and photophobia.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Meningitis — immediate IV antibiotics + consider dexamethasone; do not delay for LP.

keyValues: O2, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, lactate, urine output
redFlags: NEWS2 ≥5 or lactate >2 — sepsis, treat urgently.
Hypotension/shock — aggressive resuscitation + antibiotics.
Fever in neutropenic/immunocompromised — treat as sepsis immediately.
management: Sepsis Six within 1 hour: O2, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, lactate, urine output.
Identify and treat the source.
Monitor response; escalate if deteriorating.
Consider immunocompromise and adjust accordingly.
pitfalls: Never delay antibiotics in sepsis to wait for cultures or imaging.
A normal temperature does not exclude sepsis — the elderly and immunocompromised may be afebrile.
Always look for and treat the source, not just the fever.

infection-control.name: Infection control on the ward
infection-control.overview: Preventing healthcare-associated infection is tested through hand hygiene and precautions. The exam tests matching the right precautions to the right organism.
essentials: Hand hygiene is the single most important measure — 'bare below the elbows', alcohol rub, soap/water for C. difficile and norovirus.
Standard precautions: gloves, aprons, safe sharps disposal, correct waste segregation, respiratory hygiene.

Transmission-based precautions: contact (MRSA, C. difficile, ESBL — gloves/aprons, isolation), droplet (influenza, meningococcal — surgical mask), airborne (TB, measles, chickenpox — negative pressure, FFP3).
Isolate patients with suspected/confirmed transmissible infections; notify infection control.
Antimicrobial stewardship: prescribe appropriately, review at 48 h, use narrow-spectrum where possible, document indication and duration.

drugs.name: Alcohol hand rub / soap & water
drugs.notes: Soap and water for C. difficile and norovirus (spores not killed by alcohol)

drugs.name: PPE (gloves, apron, mask, FFP3)
drugs.notes: FFP3 for airborne (TB, measles); surgical mask for droplet

drugs.name: Antimicrobials (appropriate)
drugs.notes: Stewardship — narrow spectrum, documented indication, review at 48 h

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient with Clostridium difficile diarrhoea.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Contact precautions + soap/water handwashing, isolate; review/stop culprit antibiotics.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient with suspected pulmonary TB.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Airborne precautions (negative pressure, FFP3) and isolation; notify infection control.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient with meningococcal sepsis.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Droplet precautions + urgent antibiotics; provide prophylaxis for close contacts.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: MRSA-colonised patient on the ward.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Contact precautions (gloves/apron, isolation), hand hygiene, decolonisation per policy.

keyValues: Alcohol rub; soap/water for C. diff & norovirus
redFlags: Suspected TB/measles/chickenpox — airborne precautions + isolation immediately.
C. difficile — isolate, soap/water handwashing, stop culprit antibiotics.
Meningococcal — droplet precautions + urgent antibiotics + contact prophylaxis.
management: Hand hygiene and standard precautions always.
Isolate and apply appropriate precautions for transmissible infections.
Notify infection control; follow local policy.
Antimicrobial stewardship: document indication, review at 48 h.
pitfalls: Alcohol rub does not kill C. difficile spores — use soap and water.
Airborne precautions need FFP3 and a negative-pressure room, not a surgical mask.
Do not forget contact prophylaxis for meningococcal contacts.

cpr.name: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation
cpr.overview: ALS is a core competency. The exam tests the arrest sequence, the shockable vs non-shockable algorithm, and the reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts).
essentials: Recognise cardiac arrest: unresponsive + not breathing normally (agonal gasps count as not breathing). Call for help, start CPR immediately.
Adult CPR: 30:2 compressions:ventilations, rate 100-120/min, depth 5-6 cm, minimise interruptions. Attach AED/defibrillator as soon as available.
Shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT): defibrillate, then CPR; adrenaline 1 mg after 2nd shock; repeat adrenaline every 3-5 min; amiodarone after 3rd shock.
Non-shockable (PEA/asystole): adrenaline 1 mg immediately, then every 3-5 min. Find and treat reversible causes.
4 Hs: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia. 4 Ts: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (PE/MI).

drugs.name: Adrenaline
drugs.notes: 1 mg IV every 3-5 min; after 2nd shock in shockable, immediately in non-shockable

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.notes: 300 mg IV after 3rd shock, then 150 mg after 5th

drugs.name: Defibrillation
drugs.notes: Biphasic 150-200 J; minimise interruption

drugs.name: Reversible-cause treatments
drugs.notes: Fluids/blood (hypovolaemia), calcium (hyperkalaemia), needle decompression (tension pneumothorax), thrombolysis (PE)

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient in pulseless VT on the monitor.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Shockable — defibrillate immediately, then CPR; adrenaline after the 2nd shock.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: PEA arrest with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider tamponade as a reversible cause — pericardiocentesis if suspected; continue ALS.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: PEA arrest in a patient post-op with signs of bleeding.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Hypovolaemia — resuscitate with fluids/blood alongside ALS.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Arrest in a patient with severe hyperkalaemia.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Treat the reversible cause — calcium gluconate, insulin+dextrose alongside ALS.

keyValues: Hypoxia, hypovolaemia, K+, hypothermia / tension, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis
redFlags: VF/pulseless VT — defibrillate immediately, do not delay for drugs.
Tension pneumothorax during arrest — needle decompression.
Reversible causes — treat them (the only way to achieve ROSC in PEA).
management: Call for help, start high-quality CPR, attach defibrillator.
Follow the ALS algorithm (shockable vs non-shockable).
Give adrenaline per protocol; treat reversible causes.
Post-ROSC: ABC, targeted temperature management, treat the cause, ICU.
pitfalls: In shockable rhythms, defibrillation comes before drugs.
In PEA, ROSC is only achieved by treating the reversible cause.
Do not forget agonal gasps count as 'not breathing normally' — start CPR.

anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis.overview: A life-threatening emergency where adrenaline is first-line and must not be delayed. The exam tests the immediate response and the post-event observation.
essentials: Anaphylaxis = severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction. Rapid onset: airway (stridor, swelling), breathing (wheeze, dyspnoea), circulation (hypotension, collapse), plus skin (urticaria, angioedema).
Immediate: remove the trigger, call for help, IM adrenaline 500 mcg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) anterolateral thigh, repeat after 5 min if no improvement.
Adjunctive: high-flow oxygen, IV fluids (for hypotension), antihistamine (chlorphenamine), steroid (hydrocortisone) — but adrenaline is first-line and life-saving.
Position: lie flat with legs raised (unless breathing difficulty — sit up); do not sit/stand a hypotensive patient abruptly.
Observe for biphasic reaction (recurrence hours later) — monitor ≥6-12 h; arrange follow-up and an adrenaline auto-injector.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (IM)
drugs.notes: 500 mcg (0.5 mL 1:1000) anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5 min

drugs.name: High-flow oxygen
drugs.notes: 15 L/min via non-rebreathe

drugs.name: IV fluids
drugs.notes: Rapid crystalloid bolus

drugs.name: Chlorphenamine (antihistamine)
drugs.notes: IV/IM 10 mg; does not treat airway/circulation

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.notes: IV 200 mg; does not replace adrenaline

drugs.name: IV adrenaline infusion
drugs.notes: After 2 IM doses with no response; senior/ICU

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Stridor, wheeze and hypotension after a bee sting.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline 500 mcg, high-flow oxygen, IV fluids; repeat adrenaline if no improvement.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Only urticaria with no airway or circulatory involvement after an allergen.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Allergic reaction (not anaphylaxis) — antihistamine, monitor; be ready with adrenaline if it progresses.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: No response to 2 doses of IM adrenaline.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Refractory anaphylaxis — escalate for IV adrenaline infusion and airway support (ICU).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Anaphylaxis patient improves but you are unsure when to discharge.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Observe ≥6-12 h for a biphasic reaction; arrange follow-up and an adrenaline auto-injector.

redFlags: Stridor, hoarse voice, or airway swelling — impending airway obstruction.
Hypotension/collapse — IV fluids + adrenaline, lie flat.
No response to 2 doses of adrenaline — escalate, consider IV adrenaline infusion.
management: Remove trigger, call for help, IM adrenaline immediately.
High-flow oxygen, IV fluids, position appropriately.
Repeat adrenaline if no improvement; adjuncts (antihistamine, steroid).
Observe for biphasic reaction; arrange auto-injector and follow-up.
pitfalls: Antihistamines and steroids do not replace adrenaline — give adrenaline first.
Do not stand a hypotensive anaphylaxis patient up — keep them flat.
Remember the biphasic reaction — observe for hours.

overdoses.name: Overdoses
overdoses.overview: Treat the patient, not the poison. The exam tests recognising toxidromes and giving the correct antidote (NAC, naloxone, bicarbonate).
essentials: Assess ABC and treat the patient, not just the poison. Identify the substance, dose, time, and co-ingestants (paracetamol + alcohol common).
Paracetamol overdose: hepatotoxic. Treat with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) if levels are above the treatment line, or if staggered/late presentation. Check the paracetamol level at 4 h.
Opioid overdose: respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils. Treat with naloxone, repeat as needed (shorter acting than most opioids).
Benzodiazepine overdose: sedation, respiratory depression. Supportive care; flumazenil only in specific cases (risk of seizures).
Tricyclic antidepressants: arrhythmias, seizures, anticholinergic features — sodium bicarbonate for a wide QRS. Serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, agitation, clonus.

drugs.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
drugs.when: Paracetamol overdose above the treatment line (or staggered/late)
drugs.notes: IV (or oral); most effective early; replenishes glutathione

drugs.name: Naloxone
drugs.notes: IV/IM; short-acting — may need repeat/infusion

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.notes: IV boluses; monitor pH and potassium

drugs.name: Flumazenil
drugs.notes: Risk of seizures in chronic users/mixed overdose — rarely used

drugs.name: Activated charcoal
drugs.notes: Not for corrosives/hydrocarbons or impaired airway

clinicalScenarios.scenario: 5 hours after a paracetamol overdose.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Check the paracetamol level and give NAC if above the treatment line (or if staggered/late).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Opioid overdose with respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Naloxone IV/IM + airway support; repeat as naloxone is short-acting.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: TCA overdose with a widened QRS.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Sodium bicarbonate boluses for cardiac protection; monitor for arrhythmia/seizures.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Agitated, hyperthermic patient with clonus on serotonergic drugs.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Serotonin syndrome — stop the offending drugs, supportive care, consider cyproheptadine (specialist).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient who took mixed drugs and is drowsy.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Support the airway and breathing; avoid flumazenil; treat specific toxidromes; involve toxicology.

keyValues: NAC if above the treatment line (4 h level)
redFlags: Paracetamol overdose — NAC urgently, don't wait for symptoms.
Opioid with respiratory depression — naloxone, airway support.
TCA with wide QRS/arrhythmia — sodium bicarbonate.
management: ABC, IV access, monitoring, identify the poison(s).
Paracetamol: NAC per protocol, check levels.
Opioid: naloxone, airway support.
TCA: sodium bicarbonate for arrhythmia, treat seizures.
Psychiatric assessment after medical stabilisation.
pitfalls: Paracetamol overdose can be asymptomatic early — always check the level.
Avoid flumazenil in mixed overdoses and chronic benzodiazepine users (seizure risk).
Naloxone's effect can wear off before the opioid does — watch for re-sedation.

post-op-complications.name: Post-operative complications
post-op-complications.overview: A deteriorating post-op patient has a defined differential (bleeding, infection, leak, PE, cardiac). The exam tests the systematic assessment and the red flags for return to theatre.
essentials: Common early post-op complications: bleeding, infection (wound/chest/urine/line), VTE, urinary retention, ileus, anastomotic leak, cardiac (MI/arrhythmia/AF), respiratory (atelectasis, pneumonia, PE).
Assess the deteriorating post-op patient systematically: ABC, observations (NEWS2), wound, drains, urine output, pain, fluid balance.
Bleeding: falling Hb, hypotension, tachycardia, distended abdomen, bloody drains — resuscitate, consider return to theatre.
Anastomotic leak: fever, peritonitis, rising inflammatory markers, usually days 3-7 — urgent CT/surgery.
Ileus: abdominal distension, no bowel sounds, nausea — NBM, NG tube, correct electrolytes, mobilise. Distinguish from obstruction.

drugs.name: IV fluids/blood
drugs.notes: Resuscitate; crossmatch

drugs.name: IV antibiotics
drugs.notes: Broad-spectrum; per local policy

drugs.name: LMWH (VTE prophylaxis)
drugs.notes: With TEDs and early mobilisation

drugs.name: Analgesia
drugs.notes: Multimodal; effective analgesia aids mobilisation and prevents ileus

drugs.name: Antiemetics
drugs.notes: With NG decompression and electrolyte correction

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Day 5 post-bowel surgery: fever, peritonism, rising CRP.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Anastomotic leak — NBM, IV antibiotics, urgent CT/surgical review.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-op hypotension, tachycardia and falling Hb with a distended abdomen.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Post-operative bleeding — resuscitate, correct coagulopathy, consider return to theatre.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-op distension, nausea and absent bowel sounds.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Ileus — NBM, NG tube, correct electrolytes, mobilise; exclude obstruction.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Sudden dyspnoea and hypoxia on day 3 post-op.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider PE — assess and image (CTPA); also consider atelectasis/pneumonia.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-op patient with new AF and tachycardia.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Common after thoracic/cardiac surgery — treat the cause, rate-control, correct electrolytes.

redFlags: Hypotension + tachycardia + falling Hb — bleeding, resuscitate + return to theatre.
Peritonitis/rigid abdomen post-op — anastomotic leak, urgent surgery.
Sudden dyspnoea/hypoxia — PE, urgent assessment.
management: Systematic assessment (ABC, NEWS2, wound, drains, urine, fluids).
Bleeding: resuscitate, correct coagulopathy, consider re-operation.
Leak: NBM, IV antibiotics, urgent CT/surgery.
Ileus: NBM, NG, electrolytes, mobilise; VTE prophylaxis.
pitfalls: A falling Hb and tachycardia are more reliable than BP for occult bleeding.
Post-op fever has a differential — don't assume it is just a wound infection.
Ileus can be prolonged — correct electrolytes and mobilise rather than simply starving.

urine-retention.name: Urine retention
urine-retention.overview: A common ward problem that is usually easy to fix but can hide serious pathology. The exam tests recognising acute vs chronic retention and the dangers of high-pressure retention.
essentials: Acute urinary retention = painful inability to pass urine with a palpable bladder. Causes: BPH, post-op (anaesthesia, analgesia), constipation, drugs (anticholinergics), neurological, urethral stricture.
Chronic retention: painless, often with overflow incontinence and renal impairment (high-pressure retention is dangerous).
Management: catheterise (urethral or suprapubic if urethral route fails), drain the bladder, measure residual volume, send urine for analysis.
After catheterisation: monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and haematuria; check renal function.
Investigate the cause: PSA, renal USS, flow studies, urology referral. Trial without catheter after treating the cause.

drugs.name: Urethral catheter / suprapubic catheter
drugs.notes: Drain <1 L at first to avoid decompression haematuria/haemodynamic shifts (protocol-dependent)

drugs.name: Tamsulosin (alpha-blocker)
drugs.notes: Relaxes prostatic smooth muscle; aids trial without catheter

drugs.name: Finasteride (5-alpha reductase inhibitor)
drugs.notes: Reduces prostate size over months

drugs.name: Treat constipation
drugs.notes: Laxatives; constipation precipitates retention

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Post-op patient with a painful, palpable bladder unable to pass urine.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Acute retention — catheterise and drain; measure residual; investigate the cause.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Painless chronic retention with overflow incontinence and raised creatinine.
clinicalScenarios.answer: High-pressure retention causing renal impairment — urgent drainage and renal assessment.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Patient with retention and new neurological signs.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider spinal cord cause (cauda equina) — urgent assessment and imaging.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Elderly man with BPH in retention after a trial without catheter fails.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Start an alpha-blocker (± 5-ARI), treat constipation, retry TWOC or plan urology review.

redFlags: High-pressure chronic retention with renal failure — urgent drainage.
Retention with neurological signs — spinal cause, urgent assessment.
Post-obstructive diuresis — monitor for hypovolaemia.
management: Catheterise and drain the bladder; measure residual.
Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and haematuria.
Investigate the cause (PSA, renal USS, urology).
Trial without catheter after treating the cause.
pitfalls: Rapidly draining a chronically distended bladder can cause decompression haematuria/haemodynamic shifts — follow local volume guidance.
Chronic retention can silently damage kidneys — always check renal function.
Retention with back pain/neurology is a spinal emergency, not a simple catheter problem.

medication-errors.name: Medication administration errors
medication-errors.overview: A patient-safety topic where the exam tests prevention (the 5 rights) and the correct response when an error happens (assess, treat, inform, report).
essentials: Common error types: wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong route, wrong patient, wrong time, omission, prescribing errors, drug interactions.
Prevent: check the '5 rights' (patient, drug, dose, route, time), use the BNF/formulary, check allergies, double-check high-risk drugs (insulin, opiates, anticoagulants, chemotherapy).
If an error occurs: assess the patient immediately, stop the drug, treat any harm, inform the patient, report the incident (datix), document.
High-risk situations: look-alike/sound-alike drugs, decimal-point errors, abbreviations, verbal orders, handover.
Report and learn from errors — a 'no blame' culture improves safety. Involve pharmacy and senior staff.

drugs.name: Stop the drug / antidote if available
drugs.notes: e.g. naloxone for opioid error, glucose for insulin error

drugs.name: Treat adverse effects
drugs.notes: e.g. anaphylaxis protocol for a drug allergy given in error

drugs.name: Reporting (datix)
drugs.notes: Not punitive — improves system safety

clinicalScenarios.scenario: You gave a patient the wrong dose of insulin.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Assess and monitor the patient (hypoglycaemia), treat harm, inform the patient, report (datix), document.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A patient is given a drug they are allergic to.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Stop the drug, assess for anaphylaxis, treat (IM adrenaline if needed), inform patient, report.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: You realise you prescribed a 10-fold overdose of an anticoagulant.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Assess bleeding risk, stop/reverse as needed, inform the patient and senior staff, report the incident.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Preventing errors during a busy drug round.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Use the 5 rights, check allergies, avoid interruptions, double-check high-risk drugs.

keyValues: Assess, stop, treat, inform, report, document
redFlags: Wrong drug/dose given to a patient — assess for harm immediately.
Insulin or anticoagulant error — can be life-threatening, urgent review.
Known allergy given — treat anaphylaxis if present.
management: Prevent: 5 rights, check allergies, double-check high-risk drugs.
On error: assess the patient, stop the drug, treat harm, inform the patient.
Report the incident and document.
Review systems to prevent recurrence.
pitfalls: Never hide a medication error — reporting protects future patients.
Decimal-point and look-alike/sound-alike drug errors are common — double-check high-risk drugs.
Always check allergies before administering any drug.

early-warning-score.name: The Early Warning Score
early-warning-score.overview: NEWS2 is the backbone of recognising deterioration. The exam tests the scoring thresholds and the correct escalation response.
essentials: NEWS2 aggregates: respiratory rate, oxygen saturations, oxygen requirement, systolic BP, heart rate, consciousness (AVPU), temperature.
Each parameter scores 0-3; the total triggers a response: low (1-4) increased monitoring; medium (5-6) urgent review; high (≥7) emergency response.
NEWS2 ≥5 is a trigger for sepsis screening. A single parameter scoring 3 also warrants attention.
Escalate promptly: call for help, use SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) to communicate.
The score guides, but clinical judgement overrides — a patient who looks unwell needs review regardless of score.

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.notes: Titrate to target

drugs.name: IV fluids
drugs.notes: Per assessment

drugs.name: Sepsis Six
drugs.notes: Cultures, antibiotics, fluids, lactate, oxygen, urine output

drugs.name: Escalation (SBAR)
drugs.notes: Structured communication to the senior/outreach team

clinicalScenarios.scenario: NEWS2 of 8.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Emergency response — call for help immediately (critical care outreach); assess and treat.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: NEWS2 of 5 in a patient with a cough.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Urgent review + sepsis screening (Sepsis Six if criteria met).

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A single parameter (respiratory rate) scores 3.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Warrants attention even if the total is low — escalate and reassess.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A patient looks unwell but the NEWS2 is low.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Clinical judgement overrides the score — escalate for review.

redFlags: NEWS2 ≥7 — emergency response, call for help immediately.
Single parameter score of 3 — warrants attention.
Deteriorating trend — escalate even if the score is not yet high.
management: Measure and record NEWS2 regularly.
Escalate per the score using SBAR.
Screen for sepsis if NEWS2 ≥5.
Clinical judgement overrides the score.
pitfalls: A rising trend matters even below the threshold — don't wait for a high score.
Incomplete observations invalidate the score — always record all parameters.
Don't let a 'normal' score override a patient who looks unwell.

venous-access-lines.name: Management of venous access lines
venous-access-lines.overview: Central lines, PICCs and cannulae cause infection and mechanical complications. The exam tests recognising line sepsis and the air embolism emergency.
essentials: Central venous catheters, PICC lines and peripheral cannulae are sources of infection (line sepsis) and complications (thrombosis, air embolism, dislodgement).
Line sepsis: fever + line in situ — take blood cultures (peripheral + line), consider removing the line, treat with antibiotics.
Line thrombosis: arm/neck swelling/pain — USS, anticoagulation, consider line removal.
Air embolism: sudden collapse, hypoxia — clamp the line, left lateral/head-down position, 100% oxygen.
Care: aseptic technique for insertion and access, daily review of line necessity, remove when no longer needed, document.

drugs.name: IV antibiotics
drugs.notes: After cultures; per local policy; consider line removal

drugs.name: Anticoagulation
drugs.notes: Per protocol; consider line removal

drugs.name: Sexual/mucosal line locks (selected)
drugs.notes: e.g. taurolidine/ethanol locks for recurrent infection

drugs.name: High-flow oxygen + left lateral positioning
drugs.notes: Clamp the line first

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Fever in a patient with a central line.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider line sepsis — blood cultures (peripheral + line), antibiotics, consider line removal.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Sudden collapse with hypoxia while a central line is being used.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Air embolism — clamp the line, head-down/left lateral, 100% oxygen, call for help.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: Arm swelling and pain in a patient with a PICC line.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Line-associated thrombosis — USS, anticoagulation, consider removal.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: A cannula has been in situ for several days with no ongoing need.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Remove it — daily review of line necessity reduces infection.

keyValues: Daily — remove when no longer needed
redFlags: Fever in a patient with a line — line sepsis, cultures + consider removal.
Sudden collapse with a line — air embolism, emergency.
Arm/neck swelling — line thrombosis.
management: Aseptic technique for insertion and access.
Line sepsis: cultures, antibiotics, consider removal.
Thrombosis: USS, anticoagulation.
Daily review; remove lines when no longer needed.
pitfalls: Air embolism is the classic 'clamp first, then position' emergency — act immediately.
Unnecessary lines cause infection — review daily and remove early.
Always culture both peripheral and line blood in suspected line sepsis.

covid-19.name: Issues around COVID-19
covid-19.overview: A systemic respiratory illness with thrombotic and secondary-infection complications. The exam tests severity assessment (silent hypoxia) and evidence-based treatment (dexamethasone when oxygen needed).
essentials: COVID-19: SARS-CoV-2 infection causing respiratory illness — spectrum from asymptomatic to severe pneumonia/ARDS. Risk factors: age, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, immunocompromise.
Presentation: fever, cough, dyspnoea, anosmia, fatigue. Severe: hypoxia, respiratory distress, bilateral infiltrates ('silent hypoxia' can occur).
Assess severity: oxygen saturations, respiratory rate, NEWS2, chest X-ray, inflammatory markers (CRP, ferritin, D-dimer).
Management: oxygen to target, dexamethasone for those needing oxygen, antivirals/anticoagulation per protocol, treat complications (thrombosis, secondary infection).
Infection control: isolation, PPE, vaccination. Monitor for deterioration.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: COVID-19 patient with saturations 90% on air.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Oxygen to target 94-98%; start dexamethasone (needs oxygen); monitor and consider escalation.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: COVID-19 patient with a rising oxygen requirement and tachypnoea.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Worsening ARDS — escalate (CPAP/HFNO/ICU); treat thrombosis risk; involve critical care.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: COVID-19 patient with pleuritic pain and hypoxia beyond the pneumonia.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider PE (increased thrombotic risk) — assess and image per protocol.

clinicalScenarios.scenario: COVID-19 patient with new fever and purulent sputum later in admission.
clinicalScenarios.answer: Consider secondary bacterial infection — cultures and targeted antibiotics.

redFlags: Hypoxia (silent) — check saturations, escalate.
Rapid deterioration or rising oxygen requirement — ARDS, ICU.
Thrombosis (PE, stroke) — anticoagulation.
management: Oxygen to target, monitor saturations and NEWS2.
Dexamethasone for those needing oxygen; other antivirals per protocol.
Anticoagulation for thrombosis risk.
Isolation + PPE; escalate to ICU if deteriorating.
pitfalls: 'Silent hypoxia' — patients can be profoundly hypoxic without feeling breathless; rely on saturations.
Dexamethasone only helps those needing oxygen — not for mild disease.
Remember the thrombotic risk — consider PE in a deteriorating COVID-19 patient.
